speechtext:
And raw wool, another
primary product. Is that in a class to be compared with newsprint? I venture to say that this government in exempting newsprint has probably lost to the treasury of Canada one million dollars a year. Why is this done? Does any hon. gentleman know why we should go to the big newspapers of *this country-many of which are very prosperous; the larger they are the more prosperous they are-and say to them "Oh we will take newsprint and we will relieve it of the sales tax" and then go to the farmers of this country and say "We have relieved the big newspapers of this tax but we will put a little more on your harrows, a little more on your lumber, a little more on your clothes, on everything you work with and wear." That is precisely the course hon. gentlemen opposite have taken. It may not be popular to say anything against the source of supply of a newspaper, but some things become a duty even though they are not popular; and I know of no reason on earth why newsprint should be put on the list of articles exempt from the sales tax and why working men should be
told "We have to tax the clothing of your children, the smock that you wear, the pail that you carry. These we burden with our sales tax; we tax also what you put on your feet, the things as well that shelter you and keep you warm; but we have to relieve the big newspapers of this country of a million dollars on newsprint." Such is the way this government comes to the rescue of the common people, those common people for whom its heart bled when its ministers were in opposition. Such is the way they show to this country that these masses, these poor people who were ground down by the old autocratic government are now cared for and tenderly helped.
Let me review what the present administration has done. This government set out, or pledged itself to set out to reduce the necessities of life, to relieve food stuffs, to relieve the instruments of production of all duties and to put more taxes on luxuries and on the rich. Tell me of one dollar it has put upon the rich. Not one dollar, not one farthing. But it has relieved the rich of duties upon luxuries. The only things that are substantially reduced-that are reduced so that the reduction will reach the consumer- are luxuries imported into this country under the French treaty. This government has reduced the duties on luxuries purchased by the rich and has added to the taxes on necessities consumed by the poor. Our ministers can say: "We have brought the duty down on embroideries but we have pushed up the sales tax on boots and shoes." True the Finance Minister has made a slight reduction in the duty on boots and shoes from Great Britain knowing as he does that only a fraction, and that a fraction of superior and expensive quality worn by the well-to-do comes from Great Britain. In the case of boots and shoes from the United States it left the duty as it was but the sales tax has been increased to 6 per cent. This government relaxed the duty on brandy, it reduced the duty on champagne; and then it now has recourse to the sales tax and requires all the people of this country to make good reductions brought into effect under the French treaty. These things our ministers have done for the users of luxuries; but they have added to taxation on the necessities of life in direct and brazen violation of the pledge they made to the people of this country. "Oh," they cried in 1921-no one so often as the Prime Minister-"the main issue in this country is the cost of living. The cost of living must come down and it cannot come down under a combination of industrial plutocracy and political autocracy which is in power at Ottawa. So let me come
The Budget-Mr. Meighen

into office, he pleaded, and I will do this thing." The cost of living curve was descending at the very time he uttered those sentences; it went on descending almost perpendicularly until he and his ministers came into power. It kept on descending until their sales tax and their other new taxes came into effect-at which time the cost of living started to rise again and has been rising ever since. The cost of living is rising now and more rapidly than in other countries. The government of the day is responsible for the ascending curve of the cost of living at this hour. "Oh," they said "more retrenchment and economy must be the order of the day. You cannot get that from a government with a war mind. The Meighen government has had the war mind, and it cannot retrench." Well, this new government is now in power and beyond what it is saving by aiding the soldiers and by what it denies to the provincial treasuries and municipalities of the country what does its economy amount to? It amounts to less than nothing. Hon. gentlemen opposite also said: "Put us in power and we will get by direct taxation what the Meighen government gets by an invisible tariff." Who does not remember the speeches of 1921? I am sure the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) does not forget them. I am sure many other hon. gentlemen-some to my left-who were here then do not forget them: We were told that while Great Britain was collecting 80 per cent of her revenue by direct taxation and less than 20 per cent from customs, while the United States was doing the same thing, we were very far from such a millennium. Ah, yes, those words are in the Liberal platform, that whole recital is in the convention platform. It denounced the government of the day for collecting so little by direct taxation and so much by indirect taxation-what the Prime Minister called an invisible tariff. What is he doing now? The present government collected last year nearly fourteen millions more by the invisible tariff, by indirect taxation. They collected twenty-eight millions less by direct taxation than we did the year before. Whereas we collected according to the administration's own figures, up to the end of our last calendar year of government, for a period [DOT] of eight months, 32 per cent by direct taxation his government collected in the corresponding eight months of 1922 just 24 per cent. What he fails to collect by direct taxation, what he fails to get by the increased revenue from customs, he piles on the back of the people of this country in the way of added sales tax.

Such is the record of this administration. I think the time is surely coming if it is not here when the people of Canada shall know very clearly just what political shilly-shally has been palmed off upon them during the last two years. I do not intend to indulge in prophecy-it is not one of my gifts, I never venture to indulge-but speaking of the present government I am safe in saying that no administration ever slipped back so far in seventeen months of power as this government has done since December, 1921. Indications are not a few that the time has come when something strong, something sound, possibly something heroic in the way of large policy has to be undertaken in this Dominion. The West is struggling against intolerable conditions. The Atlantic provinces are struggling against conditions just as full of despair-of these truths there is no doubt. Where is the government in the crisis? What is the government's proposal? Without a question there must be something done to bring the Maritime provinces of our country nearer to the centre of confederation and to the advantages they have a right to enjoy. Something must be done to give renewed courage and confidence over our western plains. If it is not done, where are we drifting? Has any one the smallest hope that within the spirit and the capacity of this government there resides the ambition, the will, or the strength to resolve the situation that is upon us? I do not think the people of this country have such hope. There must be strong, there must be sound, well-digested, plans evolved and there must be brave, true, and perhaps heroic, measures taken; and the people of Canada will increasingly long for men in office who can devise and execute those things which meet the exigencies of the hour. I think they will demand that the situation which confronts us to-day shall be met in something of the spirit and by something of the resource out of which the many crises of a great war through four years were surmounted, and by which the tremendous obstacles of the after war period were overcome.

speechtext:
I unexpectedly intervened in the debate this afternoon, and I am not sure that I can contribute anything new or fresh to it, or that I can interest the members of this House in my remarks. If it is not too late, I should like to join with hon. members who have already extended their kind congratulations to the hon. Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) on

The Budget-Mr. Maclean (Halifax)
his very successful budget and also to join in their congratulations to him upon enjoying the distinction of having delivered in this country his seventeenth budget speech. Hon. members on this side of the House appreciate very much, indeed, I am sure,, the kind remarks of the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) and the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) in reference to the Minister of Finance. The hon. Minister of Finance has given forty-five years to the service of this country, and that alone is a matter of distinction. In that long period of service he has sincerely endeavoured to serve his country and has always been a true public servant. I believe to-day that in this country people regard him as the guardian of the treasury of Canada, and they have faith in his integrity and ability to render public service.
The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) started off this afternoon by saying he was very much disappointed in the budget. He said it was not a budget at all. Well, it took him a very long time to say what he required to say about it. I do not know what the hon. member requires or what he would suggest as being the proper form of budget. I remember in the early days of my parliamentary experience it was the practice for the Minister of Finance to deliver a three or four hour address, and at the end of it the minister looked like a contestant passing the winning post in a long distance race. Fortunately for Canada and the House, and in the interest of the discharge of public business, these long speeches usually delivered in the past by finance ministers have been abandoned, and very properly so. What should a budget contain? Very few matters after all interest the public or should interest the public in a budget. They require to know the financial position of the country at the end of the last fiscal year. They would like to know, and should know, what revenue the Minister of Finance proposes to collect for the next ensuing financial year, and how he proposes to spend it, and whether he anticipates a deficit or a surplus. These are important matters which should be contained in the budget. The leader of the Opposition referred to the fact that some Lords Chancellor of the Exchequer in Great Britain had some time ago delivered very model addresses upon the financial affairs of the nation. I really do not know to what he refers, but I do know that in recent years, and upon many occasions the Chancellor of the Exchequer of England delivered his budget within half an hour. It may be that I misconstrued the
purpose of the remarks of the leader of the Opposition. Perhaps I did, but if he seriously endeavoured to criticize the budget speech as to its form, I think he was wrong, because I do submit that it contained all the essential facts which a budget statement should contain. I think probably the leader of the Opposition felt that the budget of the Minister of Finance was not open to very serious criticism. I think that from his standpoint that was the weakness of the budget. Somebody said many years ago that it was the function of an opposition to oppose, and, of course, it is hard to discharge that duty if a budget is such that it cannot well be criticized.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the budget speech was delivered by the minister some two weeks ago, and the country has had considerable opportunity of discussing it and expressing its views, and I do submit that it has been well received by the country and the Minister's political opponents outside of parliament. I think it is one that should receive the commendation of members of parlimaent, regardless of the side of the House on which they sit.
The budget statement disclosed facts which, of course, the country was very well acquainted with, namely: that our expenditures in this country are stupendous; that we must raise a very very substantial revenue by taxation and the re-statement of these facts in the budget only goes to show what a serious task confronts the government, parliament, and the people, of Canada. I do not think any Canadian could well be criticized for selfglorification of the manner in which this country, large in area but small in population, is able to carry the tremendous burden that rests upon it. I think it is a matter of which every Canadian might feel proud. We are carrying on a very expensive national establishment here, perhaps too expensive when we consider the extent of the country and the fact that the population numbers only eight or nine millions. It is a marvellous thing that so small a population is able to bear the burdens that rest upon them as taxpayers. We must, of course, in order to meet this gigantic burden, have faith n\ our country. Without that our task would be almost hopeless. We have however, to assist us in contemplating the future, the fact tnat we have the capacity to grow and expand.
If Canada were situated as Great Britain and some of the older European countries, where they find themselves fully developed and where it is impossible to increase in population, Canadians might well be discouraged. Our hearts must go out to the people of Great Britain and to the people of some con-
3002	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Maclean (Halifax)
tinental European countries in their efforts to discharge the tremendous financial obligations to-day resting upon them by reason of the war. Our future in that respect is not at all dark. As I said before, this country is capable of expansion; it is capable of maintaining millions and millions of people who yet can be added to our population. The province of Alberta, concerning which we hear so much to-day, is alone capable of sustaining a population equal to that of the whole of Canada. The province of Ontario, again, is capable of sustaining a population double that which we find in Canada. So, when we have these possibilities in mind, the future should not seem so dark and hopeless as some Canadians would have us believe it to be to-day. Rather we should look to the future with courage, and with the abiding faith that in the early years yet to come, we shall have escaped from many of the oppressive burdens which we have to face to-day.
I should like to say a few words upon another subject which has been referred to time and time again during this session, so that I feel in doing so I should almost apologize to hon. gentlemen. We have heard a great deal concerning the fact-and it is a fact-that business conditions are depressed in this country. We have heard, time and time again, remarks regarding agriculture, particularly in the western provinces. Every Canadian who has come to years of understanding and who possesses powers of observation knows what are the agricultural conditions in the West just about as well as the man living in the West to-day. We have many ways by which we can acquire that knowledge. Those conditions have the sympathy of the people of the East; they would very much prefer that their fellow-countrymen in these new sections of the West were living under more favourable conditions and that trade was more favourable. Agricultural depression exists in the East just as much as it does in the West. Perhaps, in connection with agricultural pursuits in the East, this period of depression is not so effective by reason of the diversity of the farm productions of our eastern agriculturists. Those are regrettable conditions; but they are to be found in the East as well as in the West. We shall never solve this problem by accentuating conditions existing in the western section of the country without recognizing as well that they prevail in the extreme east, and without recognizing the fact, to which I shall refer later, that those conditions, after all. are world-wide conditions.
fMr. A. K. Maclean.J
I might refer to the fact that in the great fishing industry of the Maritime provinces, they have suffered very much by reason of the fact that they have been unable to secure a market for their fish production. No tariff legislation, no efforts of governments or parliaments could have assisted them. They found that, through one condition or another, they were unable to sell their products in the markets in South America, in the West Indies, in the Mediterranean ports-places beyond the power of the arm of this parliament to reach. The same is true to some extent of the lumber industry, and of the fruit industry. It is true in Canada of the manufacturing industry as well. I know many industries in this country to-day which are being operated at a loss which loss the management deliberately assume; but they prefer to carry on at a loss, or at least, without a profit, in order to maim tain their organization and in order that unemployment shall not be increased. There is not in this country to-day a human activity that is not in a depressed condition. Nobody glories in that fact; we all suffer from it. The same conditions prevail in almost every other country in the world, and my only purpose in referring to this is to impress upon hon. gentlemen this fact, that we live in troublous days; that we are suffering from the effects of the greatest war known to human history which disturbed the whole world; and that to attempt to solve our national, local and individual problems without fully recognizing these facts is altogether futile and almost a waste of time. After all, we who are here should be leaders in forming public opinion and in assisting our electorate to understand the causes of present-day conditions. At least we should deliberately avoid any misrepresentation or evasion in presenting the facts to the people lest we render ourselves unable to carry to them a sound understanding of the problem and render them unable to assist us, who represent them, in discharging our public duties.
We must face our problems in a national spirit and with courage, and we should avoid a discussion of these matters from a sectional or a provincial viewpoint. We should stress the national viewpoint. I know this is a difficult country to govern. The leader of the Opposition almost in his closing words, wanted to know what the government was going to do for the Maritime provinces, who feel themselves economically isolated from the rest of Canada. That is an economic fact, and I doubt if it ever can be changed. This, as I say, is a very difficult country to govern. But these

The Budget-Mr. Maclean (Halifax)
provinces were bound together deliberately for the purpose of building here a nation and welding the people who were here, and the people who were to come, into a prosperous and progressive nation. I do not know that any talk or suggestion about a violation of the confederation of the provinces, or any veiled intimation of a cessation from that political agreement, will help us to solve our problems, but this incessant accentuation of provincial and local problems, without due and proper recognition of the fact that they are also national, tends to the introduction of a restless political spirit which does not bode well for the future of this country. We have had in Canada in the last two or three years a new political doctrine which preaches the economic organization of groups.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
I do not know what it is called, but I hear some voice of approval of that idea, and it sounds like a voice crying in the wilderness. I do not suppose it will have any effect on the movement, but I want to say that I disapprove of it, and so I hope, will everyone in Canada, It is economically nonsensical; it is absolutely devoid of any advantage to the country; and it can only prove to be mischievous. I believe that a great deal of the trouble in one of the provinces of Canada is due to the fact that there is an element always preaching this fallacy of economic group organization. No man who believes in the doctrine of free trade, or a moderate tariff, or who understands the fundamental principles of economics can believe in this new economic doctrine. Nevertheless I find that this doctrine of economic group organization is being promulgated in parts of western Canada. I have in my hand the Grain Growers' Guide, a publication known to hon. gentlemen, and in this particular issue there appears a resolution passed at the Alberta Farmers' parliament, I think in January last. This is the resolution:
That we hereby reaffirm our adherence to the prin-r'-ole of economic group organisation and co-operation oetween economic groups and demand that our representatives stand firm in adherence to this principle, and that they oppose any steps looking to either amalgamation or affiliation with any political party, or to the forming of a new political party by any broadening out policy.
I do not deny the right of any aggregation of men to adopt that policy and promulgate it with all the energy they may see fit; but it is my right and the right of any other hon. gentleman if he desires, to express his disapproval of it. That is all I wish to say.
I am not saying that all	of the
Progressive party sitting directly opposite me favour that; I do not think that very many	of them do-at least, I
should hope not. I might read a very effective statement, if I had time, made by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) not very long ago in which he very strongly denounced the principle behind that movement, and I think that in doing so he rendered a great service to the country. I hope that his statement will be well considered by the people to whom he addressed his remarks. One effect of political doctrines of that kind, is the development of economic phantasies of such a character to-day as would, a few years ago pretty nearly send a man to some institution; and in the course of a few years, when matters have adjusted themselves, I am sure that those men who are promulgating these ideas at the present time will come to see the folly of it all.
I made a remark a moment ago to which I wish to return. I said that our conditions had not their origin in Canada, but in Europe, and I say that Europe must recover its economic processes before this country can do the same. If that fact were realized, many of the utterances which are made from time to time in this country would receive their proper weight. I am astounded at the many prominent Canadians who sometimes come out in the public press or in company meetings and speak in what they call the optimistic strain; they regard it as a bit of wisdom to be optimistic, as they say. Personally, I have no use for the words "optimism" and "pessimism;" I never use them if I can avoid them; I am not sure that they express anything worth expressing. I think it is better to try to recognize truth as being true and falsity as being false.

speechtext: And in Russia and Germany?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

speechtext:
Yes; conditions in Russia have left a tremendous influence on all the countries of the world. Now, my hon. friends opposite are very much interested in wheat and the prices of wheat. That is the large and important production in the western provinces, and naturally they are interested in receiving a fair price that will afford them a substantial profit over cost of production. And we are all interested in that matter too. We are told that the production of wheat in the last year or two has not been profitable, and that fact we all regret. If there were any means by which we in parliament could correct that position and turn it into one that was favourable, we would do so. Under ordinary circumstances wheat ought to carry a very high price in the European markets to-day. Judged by the price of other commodities, it should be somewhere between $1 and $2 a bushel, perhaps more. But what produces the present condition? Europe desires wheat -Canadian wheat-but she is not in a position to pay for it. France and Italy are back to war-time milling regulations; in some countries the law requires that potato flour be mixed with grain flour; while in other countries the use of grain is prohibited for the making of beer. These facts are well-known to hon. gentlemen, and my only reason for referring to them is that Europe's economic condition is such that she cannot buy her normal requirements of grain, and this immediately reacts upon the wheat producer in Canada-he does not obtain the price which the world's market would fairly secure for him under ordinary conditions. Let me repeat, my only purpose in referring to this is to accentuate the fact, I have stated, and I think it is worthy of repetition, because men should not forget that our adverse economic condition is due to the economic condition of Europe to-day; and for that very reason we must be interested in international affairs.
Now, Mr Speaker, it is nearly six o'clock, and before I venture to approach another subject I wonder if it would be agreeable to hon. members to call it six o'clock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, resuming my remarks of this afternoon I 
wish to allude very briefly to a matter which has been referred to frequently during this debate and, in fact, very frequently during the session. I have reference to the matter of the emigration from Canada to the United States, which has been going on in very substantial numbers during the past year or more. The fact itself is not in controversy, because it is well known that many Canadians, during the past year or year and a half, have gone to the United States. The statement, however, I thought frequently carried the implication of government responsibility, and that something should have been done, or might have been done, by this country which would have avoided that emigration. Now, Mr. Speaker, of course, the fact is very regrettable indeed, but I know of nothing which the government of the country at the moment can do to prevent it. The conditions of the United States are most peculiar, or have been during the past year or more, particularly if one has in mind the conditions prevailing in the other nations of the world. The United States has a very large population, large and well-established industries, and her natural growth is very considerable. The labour market was supplied very largely from year to year from European countries. That, however, has been prevented in recent years by their immigration laws. The result was that there was a shortage of labour, accompanied by an inflation in wages and an inflation in some lines of production and materials, particularly building materials. That brought about a .condition of prosperity in the United States, and Canadians very naturally ask one another in these days how it is that in a country not very dissimilar to ours, lying side by side, we should find in the one an apparent prosperity, and in the other a depression in trade. While it is regrettable that so many Canadians are obliged to leave their country, I am not so sure but that the judgment of Canada in the course of a year or a little more will be that it was better that we should pass through the conditions we are now passing through than to have the inflation which the United States now has, and which in the course of a few months must collapse and be accompanied with the inevitable depression and dislocation of trade. Everybody who understands or cares to observe the conditions in the United States knows that that apparent prosperity is due to an increase in the building trade. It is also well known, and remarked by everybody in the United States who knows anything about the matter, that prices of building material and wages have recently reached such a stage that they can

The Budget-Mr. Maclean (Halifax)
proceed no further, and from day to day we notice in the press evidence of threatened strikes, and we may soon expect strikes in the building trade which will react upon this country and must end the inflation in the United States. It will not be an undesirable thing for the United States if that should happen. The reaction will affect us adversely, I admit, but looking to the future, taking a long view of things as we should in these days, it is perhaps better it should come, because the sooner will we and the United States and the other countries of the world reach something approaching normal conditions. Until that period arrives, whatever men may propose, deplorable conditions will prevail throughout the world. Therefore, I wish to say upon this point that I deny any government responsibility in this matter, and I doubt whether there is anything that we in this country could do to prevent that particular condition of affairs.
The leader of the Opposition referred this afternoon to the matter of expenditure and the balancing of our budget. I concede that this is, perhaps, the most important question in Canadian politics to-day, and of infinitely more importance perhaps than tariff or any other question which anybody might suggest. It is a question upon which we should not divide on party lines. It is a matter which affects every man in this country, the rich and the poor, the high and the humble, the weak and the strong. We, as representatives of the people, charged with certain responsibilities to whom the people of the country naturally look for some leadership, should give to the government of the day, whatever that government be, our best judgment in connection with the matter of public expenditure. I am not so apprehensive as to what should be the judgment of the government upon the question of expenditure. I am more concerned with the views of members of parliament and of the people we represent. If the government were led by the right hon. member who leads the Opposition, or if the Progressive party were on the ministerial benches, I would say of them, as I now say of the government, that I would have the greatest confidence in their desire to restrict unprofitable and unproductive public expenditure. I would also concede to them the sincere desire to balance our budget. But, as I said, I am not alarmed about the government not desiring to practise such a policy. I am more alarmed as to whether the public view is right and whether the view of members of parliament is quite proper in that respect. Some time ago we
had a discussion in this House upon the question of the Hudson Bay railway. I had intended to take part in that, but for one reason and another I did not. The views expressed by the House, or by a great number of the members, left upon me the impression and conviction that we were not properly seized of the great importance of being right upon the matter of public expenditure. There is no political or party issue in this question. The Liberal party and the Conservative party were committed years ago to this expenditure. But it does not follow that either party is bound by this promise made in the past. It is true that gentlemen directly opposite me and their supporters in their respective sections of the country were always strongly in favour of this railway project, but it does not follow that to-day they should support it.
During the debate many speeches were made, some of them occupying fully an hour, trying to demonstrate that ships could navigate the Hudson bay and the Hudson strait, just as if it were a major factor in the case. In an argument, or discussion, or controversy of that kind, any person might well admit that a ship could navigate the Hudson bay and the Hudson strait. It has been done, but that, after all, is not important. The real question is, is the Hudson bay a commercial route? Can ships be put on that route and operate profitably? Can they carry grain through by that route at a price lower than the prices which are available to-day by the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence route, or by the rail and water routes? These are questions that should be settled before anybody in this country should commit himself to-day to any further expenditure in this connection other than outlined by the Acting Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) when the matter was up for discussion.
I wish to tender this bit of advice to the government, that before this country seriously entertains the idea of completing that project, a commission be appointed to inquire into what are really important and salient facts, but which have never yet, so far as I know, been inquired into at all. As I said before,-the question of navigability of the Hudson bay is not a very important factor. Of course, there must be water there; conditions must be such as to permit of a ship leaving the Hudson bay port and proceeding thence to Europe. I will concede that now as being possible; but I would not concede it to be a commercially feasible route or one worth spending any more of the public money upon,

unless it is demonstrated in a more ample way than it has been up to the present moment that it is a sound, commercial, transportation route.

speechtext: Does the hon. member not think that, in the case of a port that is one thousand miles nearer to Liverpool than Montreal, the onus of proving the commercial feasibility lies upon himself?

speechtext: I should not think so, to be fair to my hon. friend. I should say that, prima facie, every man who wishes to reflect upon the question at all, would conclude that the other route was the cheaper of the two, because there must be, in the first place, a large capital investment to provide shipping, and this must be done by the government because no private company will ever go into this enterprise. Everything indicates, on the surface at least, that you could not carry freight as cheaply by that route as by existing routes. I may be wrong; I merely say that it is sound to suggest that before the project is proceeded with further, there should be a closer examination of all the facts relative thereto.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member extend that suggestion to the Welland canal?

speechtext:
The Welland canal is in a somewhat different position, as I am sure my hon. friend will concede. I am not going to engage in an extended discussion with regard to that. There are in the western provinces instances where railway projects might very well be carried out, which would be in the interests of the country. I have heard the story of the need of railways in the Peace river country from some gentlemen who were in Ottawa recently, and I was very much impressed. When I heard the story, I could not but inquire of myself why it was that in this House amongst 235 members, there could be found men who could justify the expenditure of $25,000,000 on the Hudson Bay railway, and, perhaps, hesitate to urge an expenditure to construct in the western provinces some short pieces of railway which would do very much for those * particular localities and for the interest of the country generally.
Talking about expenditure, I should like to make to the Minister of Finance a suggestion wherein he might save some money, and I am sure if he would carry out my suggestion, he will find that it is a sound one. According to the evidence before the House, it would appear that the operations of the CanafMr. A. K. Maclean.]
dian Government Merchant Marine last year netted a deficit of six, seven or eight million dollars.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nine million dollars.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nine million dollars. That is a very substantial sum of money. I am opposed to the continued operation of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. In the first place, it is costing us nine million dollars a year, and the people of this country have to be taxed that much to meet that deficit. It renders no service to Canada, for the reason that ships could be found elsewhere, owned by private persons and companies, wdiich would perform the services just as well and as cheaply as the Canadian Government Merchant Marine is doing. I am not criticizing the policy of the government that inaugurated the programme of the construction of ships; in fact, I was a member of that government, and in that respect I am not in a different position from that of anybody who was in parliament at that time. Everyone who was in parliament at that time supported that policy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At the beginning.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At the beginning, it was deemed sound national policy. Almost every country in the world embarked upon a similar policy. I do not intend, however, to engage in any lengthy argument upon the merits or demerits of that scheme. I wish merely to point out to the Minister of Finance a method by which he may save eight or nine million dollars a year and do no injury to any public service or public interest.
The leader of the Opposition this afternoon criticized adversely the fact that the Minister of Finance predicted a deficit in the financial operations of the government for the present fiscal year. The Minister of Finance anticipates quite a substantial surplus of revenue over all oi dinary, capital and special expenditures; but he anticipates again that the railway deficits will more than consume that surplus. The leader of the Opposition says that this country should be taxed to meet that deficit caused by the railway operations, so that the budget would balance. I admit there is something in that. The Minister of Finance was very frank about the matter when delivering his budget. All reflecting people will acknowledge the desirability of balancing budgets. That is one of the troubles of Europe to-day: Their expenditures are greater than their revenues, and they meet the situation by printing paper

The Budget-Mr. Maclean (Halifax)
money, ruining themselves, ruining other countries, impeding the restoration of trade processes as between countries and countries. I think our record in Canada up to date in this respect has been a very creditable one; in this respect, as in most other respects, Canadians have held their heads well during the trying period from the armistice down to the present day. We have done nothing in this country to impede the restoration of trade channels between this country and all other countries. In this respect we are quite unique; we are almost the only country in the world that has not enacted legislation specifically designed to impede trading between countries.
No other country is in quite the same position as we are in respect of our transportation system, and it is a serious matter to tax the people of Canada these days for railway deficits. This might be a good way of informing the Canadian people in a few, short years whether government ownership and operation is a good thing or not. It is, however, the judgment of the country that the government-owned system should be given a fair trial. I would look upon the advances made to the road as a loan, or advance, and not, strictly speaking, as a part of our budget ordinary. That view may be open to some criticism. I hope the day is not very far off when this country will commence to grow and its business expand, when our population will be such that our debt will be practically cut in two, while the railway business will have grown to such an extent as not only to pay its operating expenses but to repay to the government some of the advances that have been made to it, or it will be able to finance itself by the sale of bonds and through the proceeds of such bonds restore those advances to the government. Therefore, I am not inclined to agree with the criticism of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) that the railway advances must necessarily, at the present time at least, be met by taxation. It is quite true that policy could not long be continued; neither can we long continue owning and operating a government system if it entails such a huge deficit as we have had during the past few years, because we should soon reach the limit of our capacity for taxation for that or any other purpose, and some other solution would then have to be discovered.
The leader of the Opposition this afternoon inveighed strongly against the government on its tariff policy and its failure to live up to the party platform drawn up in 1919. This matter was discussed very thoroughly at the
last session and I do not know that I can add anything to what has already been said, either by myself or by any other hon. member. I think that altogether too much importance is attached to it. Many good and distinguished men in the past have reversed their positions in respect of public policy, and in that reversal have received the applause of the country which they were serving. Hon. gentlemen will remember that Sir Robert Peel, an eminent British statesman, at a certain period in British history was opposed to the repeal of the Corn Laws.

speechtext: Does the hon. member admit that the government has reversed its policy?

I do not see any necessity for this laughter and I hope there is more behind it than appears to me at the moment. No; I did not say that the government had reversed its policy, but I did observe that very frequently eminent gifted public men have reversed almost in a moment their position on certain public questions and have not been maligned for so doing. In their lifetime perhaps they were charged with inconsistency and with having abandoned their position for purely political gain, and it required the passage of days, perhaps years, to have justice accorded them. I mention this merely to suggest in very general terms that the public should not require an inflexible stand by public men on any question. Surely there should be some room for variation in their opinions on such questions if the changes, the conditions and the circumstances of the times justify or warrant it. That was the point I wished to make, and I am sure that hon. gentlemen opposite, who were laughing a few moments ago, will not disagree with it.
Now, Sir, I was not at the Liberal Convention of 1919.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

speechtext: Yes, you would.

speechtext:
Therefore perhaps I can speak with a little more freedom in this regard than can some of the hon members who were present at the convention.

The Budget-Mr. Maclean (Halifax)
The tariff policy enunciated at that convention is not before me at the moment, but in general terms it declared in favour of an increase in the British preference and for substantial reductions on specified articles. I do not hesitate to say that it is unwise for any party convention to write a tariff schedule. It is not their business and they cannot do it; and I should say very frankly and emphatically of the Liberals who were gathered together at that time-I know them, and I do not want to say anything that is not inspired by kindness so far as they are concerned-that they could not possibly have been in a position to write a tariff schedule then. It was their duty to declare themselves upon matters of policy and nothing else. I say the same thing, too, about the policy, the platform, of hon. gentlemen opposite; they were equally foolish. If those hon. gentlemen came into office to-morrow they could not carry out their programme; and if I were to lead them through that door yonder, one by one, I am sure they would agree with me in that statement. I should hardly expect them to do so collectively before the piiblic, however. I have not the slightest doubt that in regard to their policy pretty nearly every hon. gentleman opposite me disagrees emphatically with one or more of the planks of their platform; I have too high an opinion of them individually and collectively to believe otherwise. At the same time I am not criticizing the main principle running through their platform, and I repeat that political parties are perfectly within their rights and are only performing their duty by the public in a proper manner when they declare themselves on certain principles in relation to public policy. But they have no right to deal with details, and if they do so they are bound to find themselves in serious trouble later on.
I might say more about hon. gentlemen of the opposition. There is not much use in their declaring before the public that they have been always consistent either as regards their general programme or in respect of its details. Take the tariff declarations of the Liberal-Conservative party, called the National Liberal and Conservative party; you could put anything into it or take anything out of it, and probably it was designed to facilitate operations of that kind. At the same time, however, it is only fair to say that the Conservative party have been consistently strong protectionists. Now, is it not easy to discern a distinction between the tariff policy of the Liberal party, say, and that of the Conservative party in Canada?
fMr. A. K. Maclean.]

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know that my hon. friends who say, "no", do not mean it, but they cannot provoke me away from my argument by such an interruption. The Conservative party have been consistently protectionists, except for slight variations and departures at certain times when it appeared politically advantageous to them to make a detour. They use very old-fashioned arguments in support of protection and if I were supporting a tariff policy I would find a better ground on which to advocate it. Last evening an hon. gentleman in the Conservative ranks spoke somewhat in this way: "If we buy goods in a foreign country we send our money away to help build up that country." Well, that is the idea of an antediluvian; I could make a better protectionist speech myself, or at least I could give more convincing arguments in favour of protection. That is absurd, because we do not send money away. If we send goods away we have to get goods back; the imports and exports must in the main balance. We must have trade; and a lot of this loose thinking is perhaps due to the fact that it is not countries who buy and sell; it is only people who do so. Why, the leader of the Opposition during the general election in 1921 had prominently exposed upon his political literature a statement attributed to Abraham Lincoln, that if you buy from abroad you have the goods, but you have lost your money; but if you buy at home you have your goods and you have your money too. As a matter of fact, Lincoln never said so, because he was always too wise and too well informed upon economics. I only refer to this to show that the Conservative party are- I was going to say poor thinkers. But they are pronounced protectionists now, and if their statements are to be believed they expect to remain so, because they do not think it is wise for us to trade with the people of other countries, or perhaps, speaking more accurately, they do not believe in the people of Canada doing business with anybody else; for that is what it gets down to.
What is the position of the Liberal party? It may be quite true to say that while Liberal ministries have been in power we have had an element of protection in our tariff. Hon. gentlemen opposite say if they came into office there would still be an element of protection in the tariff. They have said that time and again. It is in their platform. Even in their amendment to the budget they recognize the probability of that element being continued; but they say protection

The Budget-Mr. Maclean (Halifax)
should not be granted unless the applicant comes before a parliamentary committee and makes good his request for protection. That is simply the tariff board idea. They have it in the United States, and it is, I think, a pretty good way of perpetuating protection. I would hardly agree to it myself. At the same time, I think I am well within the mark when I say that Liberal governments have from time to time reduced the tariff, that they have always expressed the view that the principle of protection is wrong and that it should be the aim and purpose of the people of every country to some day reach a free trade basis. It is a mental outlook if it is nothing else.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

speechtext: A man may believe in the efficacy and soundness of free trade or low tariffs and yet find it impossible of accomplishment by reason of the past economic policy of his country, or by reason of conditions of one kind and another which are beyond his control. There is no occasion for my hon. friend opposite to laugh. I am not propounding any new philosophy; they themselves believe in it. For instance, during the past few weeks I was surprised to find so many hon. gentlemen among the Progressive group urging that we should carry coal from Alberta to Ontario. I have not much faith in the proposal myself, although I think it is well that it should be studied so that in the event of a recurrence of conditions such as prevailed last year in relation to our coal supply the government would be ready to meet the situation. The average member from Alberta to-day, I suppose, would support the policy of taking coal from Alberta to Ontario, but at the same time he and his colleagues know it can only be done by adding to the railway deficit and taxing the people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do you think it would be a good idea to withhold criticism until after the conference at Winnipeg and until the committee have made a report?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
ther I expect quite such prompt action on the part of the people of this country. I do not know whether the need for freedom is quite as great as it was in the Great Britain of that time when people, through protection, were reduced to starvation. But I do say that I believe the people of this country are not going to be satisfied with a mere attitude of mind concerning the trade question, but that action and reasonably prompt action will be required. That leads me to what I have to say in this matter.
I purpose, Mr. Speaker, to vote for the amendment moved by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), and I purpose to vote against the budget. When I next resume a seat in this House I purpose to sit where is the nearest approach that we have to the cross benches. My observations to-night will be directed not to an apology for, but in justification of, the action which I purpose to follow. I crave your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, in advance for the use which I shall be obliged to make of the first personal pronoun. Perhaps as I am dealing with my own conduct, that may be an excuse.
First of all, I wish to say that I am a Liberal and was never more a Liberal than I am to-night. I believe in the necessity of Liberalism. I believe the ills of this world can be healed, and healed only by the application of Liberal principles, but I want to see those Liberal principles applied with courage and with promptness. Just as we may find religion summed up in a few words, so we shall find the essence of Liberalism in those watchwords of the past, the watchwords of the Whigs of days gone by, the watchwords of the Liberals of days gone by-"Peace, Retrenchment and Reform," "Free Trade, Peace, Goodwill amongst the Nations," "Trust in the people, qualified by prudence; in opposition to distrust of the people, mingled with fear." We find the necessity for the application of what Mr. Lloyd George has recently characterized as a good definition of Liberalism: "Fair play for the under dog." That is what we need in this country. I have no apologies to make in this House or elsewhere for my conduct as a Liberal and a Liberal party man.
As a schoolboy, I became possessed of the illogical absurdities of the protectionist principle and protectionist practice, and I joined myself to the party which at that time stood ler lower tariffs, which had denounced in eloquent terms the very principle of protection and which had said that protection was legalized robbery, I do not use the language of extremeness at this time, but that was the lan-
guage used at that time by Liberal statesmen. As a college youth, I took an active part in the election of 1896 in the county which I now have the honour to represent in this House. As a result of the efforts of the Liberals in that county, there was returned to this House, after an absence of some five years, that good, sound public servant, the late Hon. Sydney Fisher. I rejoiced when the Minister of Finance made the cuts that he did in his Tariff Act of 1897. I supported his British preference and his various extensions thereof. I hoped, as all other Liberals in the country hoped, for the success of the reciprocity negotiations that went on in 1897, and I was sorry and disappointed when they failed.

speechtext:
No, in 1897 there was a commission which sat at Washington with Lord Herschell as its chairman, which endeavoured to get reciprocal relations with the United States. That failed at that time through no fault of the Liberal government. I frankly admit that I was never perfectly satisfied with the advances which were made after about 1900, when the British preference came into its full effect. After that we madu little, if any, advance in the low tariff direction. I admit frankly that the government was always face to face with the pressure from the vested interests of this country who, in the elections of 1900, 1904, 1908, were clamouring for what they were pleased to call adequate protection. The party, I suppose, is entitled to some credit for not having given way to that, though some way was given, and the schedule on some textiles was raised in 1904 or 1907, I forget just which.
When the reciprocity campaign of 1911 took place, I practically closed my law office m Montreal and threw myself into the fight with every atom of enthusiasm and power which I possessed. I believed that we were making a great forward step for Canada in that reciprocity election. I do not know just how much credit must be given to those who beat us in that election by their opposition to reciprocity. Other matters came in; sectarian cries were raised; racial cries were raised, and in the province of Quebec anti-imperial cries were raised. As a result, we lost the election. But in my humble opinion, one of the reasons why we lost that election was because, from about 1900 to 1911, we failed to preach our Liberal doctrine on trade matters. Prior to 1896, every election in Canada was a course in political economy conducted by such men as Cartwright, Mulock, Fisher, and Liberals of the old school. When we got

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
into power, the government was busy with other matters; the country was developing at a great rate; railway questions employed the energy and the mind of the government to a large extent; but we failed to preach our gospel, and the Nemesis which overtakes any church, or any body of men, or any political party that fails to preach its gospel, overtook us. There had come to the polls, there had reached maturity, thousands, if not tens ol thousands and hundreds of thousands of young men who, when 1911 came, had never heard the trade question discussed, who did not know the difference between the principle of protection and the principle of free trade, who never understood that trade in itself was a good thing, and who, therefore, were ready victims to the flag-flapping campaign that went on and the appeal to anti-American sentiment which, unfortunately, was raised by many Conservatives of that day with the slogan of "No truck or trade with the Yankees."
After that happened, I came into close personal touch with the leaders of the Liberal party of that day, especially with the Hon. Sydney Fisher and with that great Liberal statesman, the revered and deeply beloved chief of the Liberal party, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I remember in May, 1912, he came to Montreal to a great meeting. We had been beaten a few months previously, in September 1911. On that occasion there were not found wanting protectionist Liberals of Montreal who begged the old chieftain to forget all about reciprocity and to put it among the disused things back upon the shelf and say nothing about it. And what was his reply to their entreaty? I remember, as if it were yesternight, there stood the white plumed knight who said that reciprocity was a good thing, that the people of Canada had made a grave mistake in rejecting it and that they would some time wake up to the conclusion that they had erred; and then with a gesture he said: "My orders not to win or lose; my orders are to fight." It was imbued with that spirit that I went on doing all that I could for Liberal principles and the Liberal party, believing that the Liberal party was an instrument for the putting into action of those principles; and it was not very long until my principles, and my adhesion to my chief and to the Liberal party, were put to a very severe test in the election of 1917. Now, I have no criticism to offer of those men whose mind and conscience led them to leave Sir Wilfrid Laurier on the conscription issue. My mind and conscience led me to a different conclusion, and while some left him, I was among those who stood fast by
the old chieftain; and when the storms, nay, the tornadoes of sectarian hatred and racial antagonism descended upon the head of him who had always stood for broad toleration and a deep and pure Canadianism,-descended upon him because he was French-speaking and a Roman Catholic,-I considered that only an additional reason why I, an English-speaking man and a Protestant, should stand firm by his side.
Why do I vote against this budget? I vote against it because I believe after a careful consideration that it is not a Liberal budget. It is a protectionist budget with a strong Maritime province flavour.
