speechtext:
When I say "Maritime flavour" I mean that it proposes the unwise provision that goods which in the natural course of events would come by sea-carriage, which is much cheaper than land-carriage, to Portland, Maine, and thence over our own railway to Montreal, a distance of less than 300 miles, shall be discharged at Halifax and come by land carriage, a much more expensive way of transportation, over 841 miles. That is what I refer to. If it were the mentality of the Nova Scotians that I was thinking of, then gladly would I say that it was not only tinctured but saturated with a Maritime flavour. I am just wondering whether this is a party budget at all; I am wondering whether it is a budget brought forward by a party. What is a party? A party is a group of men who have decided to advance the public interest along certain lines which they hold in common. I have studied the budget carefully but for the life of me I cannot see the common principle that animates it. I never was a good man at physics, but if I remember one principle of physics it is that any body of matter, operated on by equal powers of attraction in diametrically opposite directions, just about stays where it is. And that is true of this budget. Let us examine it. Before I deal with the budget, however, permit me to speak for a moment concerning the resolution, which I am going to vote for, and in respect of which I shall make some remarks of a somewhat critical nature. The senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), with the legal acumen which is the distinguishing characteristic of the profession he adorns, has already pointed out a clause which I had noticed as one liable to give considerable embarrassment in the future. After saying that while recognizing that changes in fiscal policy should be made in such a way as

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
to give industries affected a reasonable opportunity for readjustment, it goes on to say:
This House is of the opinion that the principle of protection as a basis for fiscal policy in Canada is unsound, and that every claim for protection should be heard publicly before a special committee of parliament.
I do not like that. There is an undesirable inference to be drawn from it which I do not think was in the minds of those who drafted the resolution; I am sure it was not. If a protectionist manufacturer were represented by a lawyer as able as the senior member for Halifax, then that inference is undoubtedly the one that he would draw from that clause of the resolution. I wish it to be distinctly understood that when voting for the resolution I do not bind myself to give any consideration to claims for protection. I think we have got far too much protection, and I want to get rid of protection, not add to it, no matter how many public inquiries are held.
I am not at all sure that it was wise to have drafted the clause in the way in which it is drafted in which reference is made to reciprocity in trade with the United States as outlined in the proposed Reciprocity agreement of 1911. I am quite in favour of reciprocity, and I would have the Reciprocity agreement of 1911 if we could not get a better one. But that clause of the resolution looks as though it merely depended upon us whether reciprocity would go into effect or not. I think it would have been better to say that every effort should be made to obta'n such a reciprocity agreement.
I do not know that all the methods for raising the revenue, if such a resolution as this were adopted, have been explored. I think we should carefully consider the possibilities of a tax on unearned increment of land. We should carefully consider whether there should not be a federal succession duty tax on very large estates. These however are questions of detail, and the principle of the resolution is one which I can enthusiastically approve. It denounces protection and gives a reasonable opportunity for readjustment; it looks to what I believe is the only way in this country in which we can get out of our political and economic difficulties. We have been trying for fifty years to make ourselves wealthy by restriction; it is about time that we changed the plan and freed the energies of the people in order that they might be enabled to secure that wealth which the natural resources of the country, and their own enterprise and intelligence, should place within their grasp. As regards the proposals for reciprocity, I approve of them, but I do not 
know that they are necessary. Section 8B of the minister's resolutions provides:
The Governor in Council may authorize any minister of the Crown to enter into negotiations with any authorized representative of the government of the United States .with a view to the making of a commercial agreement between the two countries on terms that may be deemed mutually beneficial. Any agreement so made shall be subject to the approval of the parliament of Canada.
I have just one or two observations to make upon this resolution. I am in hearty sympathy with the idea, but I wonder whether it is necessary to have it declared that it is within the power of the Governor in Council to authorize any minister to negotiate a reciprocity arrangement or treaty. Surely it is always within the powers of the government to delegate one of its members for such a purpose. I note that this arrangement would be subject to the approval of the parliament of Canada. I would like to say this: If the protectionist mind continues to be developed as is likely by the present budget, what is there to prevent a repetition of what happened in 1911, when we got the Reciprocity agreement from the United States and found that the Canadian people had forgotten what was good for them and voted it down?
It is quite true that we have had offers of this sort before. If I mistake not, Macdonald put an offer of this sort upon the statute books of Canada, and it remained there until it was withdrawn in about 1898. Then, strange to say, the Americans in 1911 passed legisiation, which remained in force for about ten years, in fact until a few months ago, in which they made an offer to us. Unfortunately the wills of the parties never met, as we lawyers say. What was required was a national broker to bring the parties together. And what we require in Washington to-day is an ambassador to represent Canadian interests there all the time, to drop the word in due season as to the advisability of close commercial relationship between the two great nations which occupy such a large part of the North American continent.
Now, we have had some sort of reciprocity with the United States, as the right hon. leader of the Opposition said in his remarks this afternoon. But while we are offering reciprocity, I would draw the attention of the House to the fact that there is reciprocity in certain lines now within our grasp. Boots and shoes and leather go free into the United States. Why therefore should they not come free into Canada? In connection with this matter the member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), whose remarks I always listen to with the greatest of pleasure and attention, said there were manu-

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
facturers in his riding who were prepared to have reciprocal trade relations with the United States if we could guarantee them permanence. I may say parenthetically that I visited his home town some months ago and I never was in a more beautiful town of its size, surrounded by fields so well cultivated that they gladdened the heart, and with every indication of hard work, thrift and brains among its people. Well, if it was possible for those manufacturers to open up lines of business with a few customers who might drop off in three or four years I wonder whether they would say, "We do not think we will bother going after their business; it lacks permanence." Would they say that? I do not think they would. And let me contrast their attitude-which I have no doubt is correctly described by their distinguished representative-with the attitude of the stock-raisers of the West who had a cargo of stockers landed on the dock at Bristol, I think it was, almost as soon as the British cattle embargo was lifted. Why was it, Mr. Speaker, that this provision of the American tariff allowing boots and shoes and leather to enter the United States free has been on their statute books since the 3rd October, 1913, if I mistake not, without its being availed of to any great extent by our manufacturers, while the cattle embargo was not off a day before a cargo of stockers was landed at Bristol? What is the difference? Were these stockraisers better business men than the manufacturers of North Waterloo? No, I do not believe so. But they were driven on by the urge of economic necessity to avail themselves of the very first chance to get into {mother market. They had no home market which would under ordinary circumstances absorb their product, and therefore as gallant adventurers and capable business men they had to look abroad in order to find customers.
The same thing affects agricultural implements; these can go free into the United States. Then there is in the American tariff provision whereby certain materials, for which at the present time there is a tremendous demand in the United States, may enter the American market free or at such rates of duty as will be imposed on similar goods coming into Canada from the United States. I refer to building brick, calcium carbide and its by-products, and cement. Now, there is no question about the building boom in the United States. I notice in the papers that bricklayers in that country are not satisfied with twelve dollars a day; they have struck for more. Why should not our brick and
cement manufacturers who are situated in positions where they can readily ship their products into the United States market take advantage of their opportunities? The movement of brick and cement is largely controlled by the freight rate, and where the Canadian manufacturers of these commodities can have them carried by water, or where they can have the advantage of a cheap freight rate, surely it should be the business of government to let them get the advantage of trading across the line.
Now, let me deal for a short time with the budget itself. I would hate to be unfair. The government deserves great credit for reducing the duty on both raw and refined sugar. That reduction should be of some advantage to the Canadian consumers of sugar. But the budget reminds me of the vicissitudes of human life-there are so many ups and downs in it. Hemp for agricultural purposes goes on the free list; licorice paste not sweetened goes down to 10 per cent, 15 per cent and 17J per cent, as against 15 per cent, 20 per cent and 20 per cent under the old tariff. Raisins and dried currants go up in the scale, and so do potatoes.
Now, although I live in Montreal I represent an Eastern Townships riding. There one of the national dishes is raisin pie, and why the wives of the farmers whom I represent should be obliged to pay more for the raisins that go into their pies in order that Australian raisins may come from-I do not know how many thousand miles, but I suppose at least six thousand; it took the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) a considerable time to go there and come back -why raisins that come from California should be excluded by a tariff which has been increased by about 300 per cent in order that raisins from the other side of the world may be brought in is, I suppose, part of that mania for interfering with the free play of commerce, which I expect will be sweetened and blessed by the slogan of "Imperial Solidarity" or something of that sort.
I do not need to talk about the duties on artificial silk. Artificial silk has become a protected article, on the old protectionist theory that every process through which material goes should add something to the duties. I am not going to read all the different processes and all the different rates of duty; the duty starts at one end at 10 per cent and ends at the other at 37J per cent. I will not delay the House long with any remarks on the bounty on hemp or remarks on the bounty on copper: I am of the opinion that every rope should hang by its own
301S

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
strength and that every copper tub, as well as every other tub, should stand on its own bottom.
Why am I opposed to this budget? Because as far as I can see any governing principle in it, it is the principle of protection. I could not quite see the force of all the bitterness in the remarks of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) this afternoon. He should be rather pleased; this administration has come to agree to his fiscal views-there does not seem to be much difference between them on this budget. That is a matter, I should think, for congratulation, if the right hon. gentleman is really sincere in his protectionist views. But I sometimes wonder when I listen to his splendid eloquence and observe the operation of his analytic mind, whether he really is protectionist; it would seem strange if he were.
What is the problem that faces the Canadian people to-day? Half our people live on the land; a great deal more than half the people, probably three-quarters of them, either live on the land or directly depend upon those who do. And what is the situation in regard to our farmers? Of course, they can improve their methods. I understand the view of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is that if only we could all go in for mixed farming, all would be well. I am quite willing to admit that farmers could improve their methods, that they may be able to get better prices for their products without getting more from the consumer, by following out proper methods of co-operative selling. And perhaps if the rings and combines will allow them-and there are such, although the right hon. leader of the Opposition scoffs at the idea-they may get some things cheaper through co-operative buying. But that will not affect to any very great extent this great difficulty: that the farmer sells his products at prices which are somewhat under wholesale prices, and has to buy the commodities which he needs in retail quantities at prices enhanced by a protective tariff in many cases and by the rings and the selling agreements which exist, to a greater extent than they otherwise would, under the tariff. That is the great problem of the farmer. I do not propose to enter into any long disquisition about the theory of free trade and protection, for I would weary you; you have listened to long speeches and interesting speeches to-day. I am opposed to the principle of protection. I do not propose to wipe it all out over night; I do not propose to do anything extreme, but I propose, if I possibly can through my feeble efforts, to 
get action. I am opposed to the principle of protection because it has proved itself in this country a most dismal failure. I do not think anybody will deny that we have an honest, a thrifty, a hard-working people. We have good men and good women in Canada. We have good soil, second to none for certain purposes. We have certain disadvantages: we are spread' too sparsely over the country. We have a hard winter, but not an unhealthy one. But we have not kept our natural increase, and we have not kept the immigration which we have brought in at great expense during the last thirty years. That is the situation; that is the proof of the failure of this policy.
Then, the policy is anti-national. It was called the National Policy; it is not a national policy; it is a policy which makes the trade question and the taxation question of this country nothing more than a local issue. The eloquent member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) last year stated with interesting frankness that if he lived on the prairies he would no doubt be a free trader, but as he lived in British Columbia he was a protectionist. It is not only anti-national, but it is anti-social, it gives certain people a direct interest in the incidence of taxation and makes it profitable for some people that a high debt should be maintained in this country in order that there may be a high rate of taxation. It is anti-national in that sense. The consequence is that whenever a trade question is under discussion in this House we have hon. members presenting, not a national view, but a sectional view; it is hardly possible for them to do otherwise. It makes of this House directly an antithesis of what Edmund Burke said parliament should be. May I, Mr. Speaker, quote his words:
Parliament is not a congress of ambassadors from different and hostile interests; which interests each must maintain, as an agent and advocate, against other agents and advocates; but parliament is a deliberative assembly of one nation with one interest, that of the whole, where, not local purposes-
It will be recalled that an hon. member of this House, speaking the other night on the copper bounty, did not attempt to express what he thought was the national interest; he expressed rather the view of his constituents. Let him as well as others listen to these words:
-where not local purposes, not local prejudices ought to guide, but the general good, resulting from the general reason of the whole. You choose a member, indeed, but when you have chosen him, he is not member of Bristol but he is a member of parliament. If the local constituent should have an interest, or should form a hasty opinion, evidently opposed to

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
the real good of the rest of the community, the member for that place ought to be as far, as any other, from any endeavour to give it effect.
But there is a deeper reason, Mr. Speaker, why I should oppose this budget, a reason deeper than any economic reason. I cannot regard this budget as anything else but a distinct repudiation of the representations made by the Liberal party at and since the convention of 1919, and, indeed, a falling away from the true historic principles of the Liberal party. I do not pretend that our practice has always been consistent with our profession, but I do say that as between the two great political parties of this country, the Conservative party stood for the principle of protection and the Liberal party stood for the principle of free trade, or, if not free trade, low tariff. If any one tries to represent the Liberal party as a protectionist party he is endeavouring, I think, not to justly interpret the history of this country.
Now, what was the Liberal party platform? The distinguished member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) says that those who gathered at the Liberal convention were very foolish because we laid down this platform. The member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) says that he does not think that the Liberal party should be shackled or fettered by any pronouncement on the trade question made at that convention. The member for Halifax was not at the convention, but I believe the member for North Waterloo was, and if he disagreed with the idea of laying down a platform which was one of the avowed objects of the convention, I ask him, in all sincerity and with all courtesy as one old friend to another, why he came? The Liberal platform was laid down at the Liberal convention which met in the early days of August, 1919. One reason why the Liberals called a convention in 1919 was this-and here I beg to remark that they are the only one of the two great parties which so far have held national conventions. Others have held provincial conventions, but of the great parties in the country the Liberals only have held a national convention. We held a national convention because the Liberal party had been rent in twain by the conscription issue. We wanted to all get together to draw up a policy we could all subscribe to. In general terms-I am no doctrinaire who believes in being shackled to the crossing of every T and the dotting of every I in a pronouncement of this sort-that it should be a chart and a compass, and that chart and compass should be kept in use. That is the claim I make. We gathered together from all over Canada to name our leader and to lay down
our platform. I do not think it was a foolish proceeding. May I note this: That in 1893 we did the same thing. We had a convention and laid down a platform, and we won the election of 1896 and went back into power after being out of office for eighteen years. In 1919 we laid down our platform, elected our leader and went back into power in 1921. The Liberal platform read as follows:-and I am not ashamed of this platform.

speechtext:
It was not drawn up by myself alone; it was decided upon by others as well as myself. As it was drawn first of all in a private meeting I have no right and I will not attempt to say whose hand wrote it. I was called from the General Resolutions Committee, of which I was chairman at the convention, to defend this platform from the stand on which the speakers stood. I spoke on that occasion against the Premier of British Columbia who, for some reason or another, was against, not the spirit of the platform, but certain provisions therein. A distinguished lady from Hamilton spoke against it, and a very dear friend of mine from Montreal did the same thing. Well, I spoke, it was put to a vote, and was carried by about nine votes to one as far as I could see. There was no question as to the unanimity, the substantial unanimity, of the delegates gathered there, that it was the proper platform for us to lay down. How does it read? I am sorry the right hon. leader of the Opposition is not in his seat to-night. This has not got a brown cover but it is the same platform and he would have the pleasure of hearing it read in a certainly distinct and audible voice. It reads as follows:
That the best interests of Canada demand that substantial reductions of the burdens of customs taxation be made with a view to the accomplshmg o two purposes of the highest importance; First, diminishing the very high cost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; second, reducing the cost of the instruments of production m the industries based on the natural resources of t e Dominion, the vigorous development of which is essential to the progress and prosperity of our country.
That, to these ends, wheat, wheat flour and all products of wheat the principal articles of food, farm implements and machinery, farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery and repair parts thereof, rough and partly dressed lumber, gasoline, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils, nets, net-twines and fishermen's equipments, cements and fertilizers, should be free from customs duties, as well as the raw material entering into the same.
That a revision downwards of the tariff should be made whereby substantial reductions should be effected in the duties on wearing apparel and footwear, and on other articles of general consumption (other than luxuries), as well as on the raw material entering into the manufacture of the same.

speechtext:
Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hear some people saying, "hear, hear" to that statement. Let me read to those who say "hear, hear" the words of that great English Whig statesman, Edmund Burke, who possibly laid down as correctly as was ever laid down, the relationship which should exist between member and constituents. Edmund Burke said, in addressing his electors at Bristol:
Certainly, gentlemen, it ought to be the happiness and glory of a representative to live in the strictest union, the closest correspondence, and the moist unreserved communication with his constituents.
I break off my quotation to state to you, Mr. Speaker, and to my fellow members, that I have followed that plan. Since I have been a member of this House, every session I have gone back to my people and held meetings with them. After one session I had one meeting when I had the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) with me, and we had such a large meeting on that occasion that I did not think it necessary to hold another during that recess. But after each ses'-sion I have held meetings, from that one meeting to other times when I have held as many as thirteen in a small riding, the smallest riding in Quebec. I maintained a close co-operation and correspondence with my electorate, and anything I did in this House I reported to them. I think, on the whole, I generally obtained, without any formal resolution or anything of that sort, their approval of what I had done. I may say that in this case I had no time to go and consult my electorate to any extent, even though the obligation had been upon me. I saw the chairman of the organization in my riding; and while I had not time to talk to a number of my electorate, I [DOT] talked with a few of them. Though they may regret that I find it incumbent upon me to take a seat which will be an outward and visible sign that I am not in sympathy with the administration on their budget, on the whole I believe they are willing that I should do as my mind and my conscience dictate I should do. Edmund Burke continued:
Their wishes ought to have great weight with him; their opinion high respect; their business unremitted attention. It is his duty to sacrifice his repose, his pleasures, his satisfactions, to theirs; and above all, ever, and in all cases, to prefer their interests to his own. But, his unbiassed opinion, his mature judgment, his enlightened conscience, he ought not to sacrifice to you; to any man, or to any set of men living. These he does not derive from your pleasure; no, nor from the law and the constitution. They are a trust from Providence, for the abuse of which he is deeply answerable. Your representive owes you, not his industry only, but his judgment; and he betrays, instead of serving you, if he sacrifices it to your opinion...

To deliver an opinion is the right of all men; that of constituents is a weighty and respectable opinion, which a representative ought always to rejoice to hear; and which he ought always most seriously to consider. But authoritative instructions; mandates issued, which the member is bound blindly and implicity to obey, to vote, and to argue for, though contrary to the clearest conviction of his judgment and conscience,-these are things utterly unknown to the laws of this land, and which arise from a fundamental mistake of the whole order and tenor of our constitution.
It is on that ground that I take my stand. I do not propose to push a doctrine, no matter how sound, to extremes. An occasion will present itself very shortly in my riding, where I can place my whole case before my electors. If they approve what I have done, then will I gladly continue to serve them. But if they do not approve what I have done, if they wish to have in this House a Liberal who thinks more of the label on the bottle than what is in it, who will sacrifice his opinion arrived at after careful consideration and in the light of his conscience, to the desire of the whips, then I will resign my seat and allow them to elect such a one if they so desire. Then, somewhat disappointed, but neither downhearted nor disconsolate, I can go back and devote to my clients, my office and my law books some part of the energy which I have, as far as in me has lain, devoted to what I considered to be the interests of my country. I have enjoyed public service in this House and out of it; but I enjoy public service only on terms which, I believe, are consonant with the dignity of a public man, and 1 do not believe a public man helps himself. or his party, or his country by voting in a manner in which he does not believe. I repeat, I am not leaving the Liberal party; but I am refusing to support the present administration in a budget which I do not believe to be a Liberal budget. I take my seat in the corner of the chamber. I join no other party. There*, when liberal legislation is brought before this House, I will support it by my vote and, if necessary, by my voice; but I shall be in a position, if legislation which I do not think is liberal, is brought before the House, to criticize it with a greater freedom, though I trust with no lack of courtesy, than I possess when I sit amongst those who are responsible more or less for the legislation.
In closing, let me quote again that great English statesman Edmund Burke. I say it in all humility, but I believe it to be true:
My principles enable me to form my judgment upon
men and actions	The principles of true politics
are those of morality enlarged; and I neither now do, nor ever will admit of any other.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I begin to

The Budget-Mr. Marler
discuss the budget I desire to join with those hon. members who have preceded me in congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) upon having completed his seventeenth financial statement. I will go even further and say that the minister deserves to be described as a faithful public servant. It is quite true that in his budget speech he did not perhaps include certain matters which some of his supporters would like to see taken into consideration, but it is possible that the minister may consider them when his proposals are being discussed in detail. I had not the pleasure this afternoon of listening to the whole of the speech of the right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), but that part of it which I did hear impressed me as being full of ability, although I fear it lacked any generosity whatever towards the government of the day. Possibly that is not the part of the leader of the Opposition, nor indeed of the party which he leads; I do not suppose it is to be expected that they should show any generosity of feeling towards this government. I was therefore in a measure surprised when my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) in the course of*his remarks, exhibited the great magnanimity *which he did on that occasion. He said in discussing the budget that he had no amendment to offer but would leave the Progressives to put forward one on this occasion. Why did he make that observation? I wondered whether a ray of light had come into the old Tory party, or whether this was a piece of generous behaviour. I do not think it was generosity, in the least degree. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for West York seemed to me to feel great regret that he could not criticize the budget more severely than he did, so that his not moving any amendment was due to no generous impulse on his part. Our friends the Progressive party have taken a very decided view of the budget; they are very firm in their attitude towards it. They say that the policy of the present [DOT]administration is in no regard distinguishable from that of its predecessors, and by way of rider to this, they say that the system of protection is wrong in theory and in fact. They go on to say that the tariff should be lowered, tending, of course, towards free trade, or failing that, a tariff as near free trade as it can be, until free trade can be secured in this country.
I think that anyone would admit that this is about the most difficult country in the world to govern. We have a very small population sparsely spread over a tremendous area, a ribbon of land stretching from ocean
to ocean. There are certain ideas in the Maritime provinces, other ideas in Ontario and Quebec, then going over that great bridge of stone into the prairies we find entirely new ideas, and so on over the mountains to British Columbia. I do not wonder that my Progressive friends opposite should have certain views of their own in regard to questions of the tariff. I do not blame them in the least. But my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke) in his speech, which I thought was a very able one and which was full of sincerity, as the hon. member's speeches always are, made a remark which appealed to me very much; he said that the West, the manufacturers in the East, should try to get together. Well, that is precisely the policy which I think we should endeavour to bring about in Canada. It is absolutely impossible in a country of this character for the people to live apart; it is impossible to have one principle in the W'est and another in the East. After all, why should it be impossible to strike some common ground? What reason is there why the farmers of the prairies should not trust the East as the East trusts them? They say, "We cannot agree to that because the men of the East are manufacturers and they therefore want a tariff." They do want a tariff, it is quite true. But, on the other hand, do not the people of the West want certain policies as well? Surely it would be possible in due course of time for the parties to get together and arrive at one common policy which would be good for the whole of Canada. Why should one policy be advocated for one part of the country and another for some other part? How is it going to be possible for Canada to proceed under such circumstances? How would it be possible for any business in this country, whether farming or manufacturing, to prosper if we are divided as regards the desires of the country as a whole? Obviously it is quite impossible.
My friends of the Progressive party tell us that times are very hard in the West and that they are finding it very difficult to get along. That is quite true. But in reply to that it can be very truthfully said that not every business in the East is prosperous; the business men of the East are experiencing their own difficulties also. An hon. member stated in his speech that the farms are not paying, but he admitted, I believe, that certain returns showed that in the case of each of 240 farmers there was a surplus of some $600. I can assure the hon. gentleman that there are many inhabitants of the province of Quebec from which I come who can barely make a living, to say nothing at all of $600 to boot

The Budget-Mr. Marler

The difficulties are not alone on the prairies; they are not alone in the West. Difficulties are common throughout Canada to-day; but my good friends the Progressives will not consider this fact at all. Hon. gentlemen do not seem to consider the great fundamental difficulties that exist throughout the country at this time. They say they want certain policies put into effect; they want certain economic facts realized. Well, I know, and we all know very well that they do. What are those facts to which I refer? They say that one thing they want is lower freight rates. Of course the West needs lower freight rates; but the East needs lower freight rates too. But how can we have lower freight rates at this time, if at the same time we are to pay any operating charges at all on the railways? If we increase the deficits of the National Railways it simply means that they must be made up in taxation in some other form. The next thing, they say, which bears heavily upon them is the loss of the purchasing power of the dollar. That also is perfectly true; I know full well that the prices of farm products have been deflated while a great many other commodities have been inflated. But is that the fault of the government? Can this government remedy the condition quickly? They certainly cannot.
They also ask for rural credits. Well, I am certainly very much disposed to give the West rural credits if this is feasible. But, after all, is not this a subject for provincial action? Unfortunately our western friends do not take these factors into consideration. We in the East would like to see the economic evils under which the people of the West are suffering remedied where possible, but they cannot be remedied in a day-in fact some of them are beyond the power of governments to remedy. That being the case, what do my hon. friends, the Progressives, do? They bring in an amendment to the budget condemning the government because it does not introduce lower tariffs.
Now, I should like to address myself particularly to my hon. friends of the Progressive party. The hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) gave us in great detail his ideas of free trade. He said it is a splendid theory.
I agree with him, but so far as I can see it is a theory and nothing more. He did not for a moment suggest, neither did a single speaker among my friends opposite suggest, how the revenue loss from reduced tariff duties can be made up. Our tariff to-day is not a high tariff; it is on an average 17i per cent collected on imported goods. I do not call it a protectionist tariff; on the contrary, I have always termed it a development tariff. I (Mr. Marler.]
believe that we need such a tariff to encourage our industries and permit of their fullest development. What would happen if we had not a tariff of that description? Our industries in the East could not survive, they would go out of existence. My hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke) says, "All right, if they cannot survive let them go out of existence." Well, that is what is staring us in the face in the East. There is not the slightest question of a doubt that if the tariff is lowered at once, or if it is to be lowered from time to time to any appreciable extent, our industries will simply have to cease.
But supposing these industries do close up, what will happen to the people employed in them? Will they not have to leave Canada to gain a livelihood elsewhere? Will there not be unprecedented unemployment and tremendous loss? And will not the number of people as a consequence who can be taxed be gradually diminished, and the burden of taxation become all the heavier for the rest of us to bear? These results are bound to happen.
But supposing, for example we did do away with our comparatively moderate tariff, how are* we going to obtain our revenue? I have no doubt that the gentleman who drew this resolution sat down with pencil and paper and figured out very carefully how he was going to obtain his revenue, because I assume that if my hon. friends of the Progressive party succeed to office they will put this resolution into effect. I am positive that my hon. friend from Brandon will never go back on anything he says, and it follows that he and his party will implement their resolution whenever the opportunity presents itself. Well, have the hon. member and his friends sitting around him studied how they will get their revenue if their resolution is put into effect? I doubt if they have. I doubt very much if they have considered how the revenue of the country is to be maintained. What was secured from tne tariff last year? I am speaking now of the tariff purely from the view of revenue.
I am assuming that we have closed up our factories and created unemployment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has got past it, but it is only an assumption on his part that all the factories will be closed; he does not know for certain.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was waiting for an interruption from the hon. member because I want to ask him a-question in reply. Does he or does he not admit that this country can stand free trade?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
While we stand for free trade in principle, I do not think the hon.

The Budget-Mr. Marler
gentleman has heard any member of the Progressive party state that we are going to put free trade into effect immediately. Hon. gentlemen supporting the tariff always ask the question: How would you get your revenue without the tariff? Well, you could have a very much lower tariff to begin with and yet have a very much higher revenue. A protective tariff is not a revenue tariff. Twenty-two and a half per cent or twenty-five per cent straight protection does not produce very much revenue as a rule; consequently you may have a very much larger revenue with a very much lower tariff.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am very much obliged to my hon. friend for his reply. It is precisely what I wanted to get. My hon. friends the Progressives, then, do not believe in free trade.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, I did not say that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: So far so good.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, I did not say so. I believe free trade is the proper principle to be put into practice; but we are sensible people and realize existing conditions, and therefore we simply say: It is for the manufacturers to get prepared for free trade, and they should be given time to adjust their business accordingly. I have more faith in the Canadian people than the protectionists have. I believe our people have sufficient energy and ability to make their business successful without any protection whatever.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Very well. Then when my hon. friend's party come into power they would serve notice on the manufacturers of Quebec and Ontario and the rest of the Dominion: We are going to lower the tariff year by year, and you must arrange your business accordingly. Am I correct in taking that to be the policy of the Progressive party?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Broadly speaking.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sorry to put these questions to my hon. friend, but I would not have him misunderstand me and I should not like to misunderstand him. I can assure my hon. friends opposite that I have the fullest sympathy and the very greatest admiration for the West. I say that with perfect sincerity. All I ask in so far as the East is concerned-and although I am not speaking to a very full House to-night I know full well that my words will be heard outside- is some reasonable tariff which will permit our industries to develop, and until our
population is very much increased we cannot do with any lower tariff than we have now. Let me add that the East has every sympathy with the West and wishes it the fullest prosperity, and would welcome any reasonable policy on which both East and West can stand together. Later on, I shall speak- possibly with the approval of my hon. friend from Brandon-on a suggestion which I have to make to the government. But I can say in all sincerity that the present tariff, in so far as can be ascertained without investigation, is needed in order that we may retain our industries and ensure their development in harmony with the growth of the country. We cannot compar^ the industries in our little country cf lesg^han nine million people with the industries in the States which my hon. friends of the Progressive party are so fond of referring to for comparison. Do my hon. friends know that the mills in the province of Quebec have to run on very many lines of goods so that each product consequently costs much more to manufacture, whereas in the United States a single mill is run year and year out on one line of goods alone?
One hon. gentleman opposite some days ago compared the prices i_. the United States with the prices here. I know that the prices in the United States are lower than they arc-in Canada; they are bound to be. We cannot manufacture things at the prices at. whicn they are manufactured in that country. Take down your tariff and you will close up your factories, drive all capital out of Canada, keep people away-that is what you are facing if you cut your tariff down too low. The hon. member for Brandon will say, "Oh, we are not going to do it all at once." Perhaps not; I would not accuse hon. gentlemen opposite of doing any rash thing; they are not that type of men. I believe they are all sincere and honest men, but they would serve notice on businesses that the tariff was coming down, and that would create an unsettled state of mind among those carrying on business in the province of Quebec, in the East generaily with the result that those businesses could not progress.
Let me come back to the question of how we are to obtain the revenue. There wai collected last year in tariff duties $133,000,000. I was going on to say when I digressed a few moments ago that I assumed whoever drafted this resolution, whoever is to be minister of finance when the Progressive party gets into power, carefully studied out how that $133,000,000 should be made up. It is suggested in this resolution that in order to provide for
The Budget-Mr. Marler

revenue to take the place of the tariff, there should be an extension of the income tax which would bear more heavily on unearned incomes. Now I am quite positive-and J trust I do not overstate the case-when I say it is utterly and absolutely impossible to make up $133,000,000 in income tax at all. It is next to impossible to make up half that amount from income tax. I will tell you why, because I figured it out myself with the very greatest of care in order to see if I could read into this resolution any possibility of taxing what are commonly called unearned incomes. The term "unearned income" is used very loosely-sometimes to designate the accumulations which a man I^as gathered together after years of labour. I do not call that unearned income. I look upon unearned income as income derived from inheritance, and receipts of that description. I do not see any serious objection, as I stated in the House a few nights ago, to slightly increasing the tax on income which is accumulated but which is not being actively earned. I see no particular objection to a slight additional tax there, and I see no objection to a considerably heavier tax on inherited income, because that is not being earned as class A income is. The total income tax collected in 1922 was $40,000,000. The amount collected on incomes up to $20,000 was roughly, $20,000,000. Now, I know that whoever drew this resolution was not trying to get after the little fellows; he was trying to get after the big fellows, the men who had large incomes; he wanted to tax them more heavily in order to replace the loss occasioned by the change in respect to the tariff. Well, I have said that in respect of incomes of over $20,000 the amount paid by way of income tax was $20,000,000. If you wish to make up only half the $133,000,000, or $70,000,000, out of these larger incomes, you have to impose a tax three times as heavy as the present tax. Now, I have made a calculation in order to show hon. gentlemen opposite the fallacy of this resolution. So far as getting your revenue is concerned it i absolutely fallacious; you would go broke m one year if its suggestions were carried out. What would happen? Let us tax these larger incomes, starting with an income of $30,000. You would have to continue the present tax of 14 per cent and have in addition another tax of 42 per cent; in other words, you would tax that income 64 per cent in order to gain one-half the amount collected last year in customs duties. On an income of $50,000 you would have to place a tax of 80 per cent; on an income of $60,000, 82 per cent, and in the case of an income of $70,000, in order to get
(Mr. Marler.]
your revenue you would have to take it all- every cent the man had by way of income. That is how increasing the income tax would work out according to the most careful calculations that I have been able to make-and I may say that I am not unused to figuring out income taxes in many ways. I suggest to hon. members that that is a matter worthy of consideration.
The resolution goes on to suggest also an increase in excise duties. Well, the amount of excise duties collected in 1923 was $35,000,000. You have to make up your $133,000,000; in other words, you are going to reduce your tariff gradually until it gets to the vanishing point and you put into practice the free trade theories that the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) propounded so ably to-night. I say that he pronounced the theories very well indeed, but he did not give you one single practical idea as to how free trade as applied to Canada would affect the people of this country or affect anybody else. In this resolution you pick on the poor old tariff, which has been made the football of politics from time immemorial. You say, "If the tariff is lowered, if the tariff is taken off, notwithstanding the fact that industries will be ruined, our lives will be saved." But what did one of your own members say the other night? He made a statement which to me was exceedingly significant. The hon. member for North Wellington (Mr. Pritchard) said that the amount of taxes paid by every person in Canada owing to the tariff was $14.68. or, for a family of five, $73.40. Now, Mr. Speaker, is the West as badly off as all that? Are your difficulties worth only $73.40 to each family? There is the statement of your own member-are you going to ruin the businesses in Quebec and Ontario for this amount? That is what you will do by this resolution if it is carried, as the hon. member for Brandon assures me in due course of time it will be. That is what is going to happen.
However, let me leave the acrimonious part of this resolution. I do not think members of the Progressive party have seriously studied the effect of the proposed amendment. They did not sit down and study and figure out as to how that resolution could be given effect to, and they run the Hanger by leaving it on the pages of Hansard of having it quoted against them some time in the future just as the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) to-night-somewhat unkindly I thought-flung into the face of the government the resolutions which had been placed on Hansard by the Liberal party. My recommenda-

The Budget-Mr. Marler
tion to hon gentlemen opposite is to withdraw that resolution.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do not flatter yourself.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not flattering myself;
I am trying to do you a distinct service.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We will look after ourselves.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Look after yourselves? I absolutely challenge my hon friend from Last Mountain to make up any budget on that resolution. I challenge him to do so. I would like to see him come before the House, and with pencil and paper figure out any budget that will make up for the custom revenue that will be lost under that resolution. The resolution as drawn is directly opposite to the interests of the Progressive party. They talk about the primary industries of the country. Here it is in black and white-the primary industries of the country. And they talk about the natural resources, those great natural resources we have all heard so much about. Why every man who has spoken in this House from time immemorial has informed us that we have the greatest natural resources of any country in the world, which I believe is true. But those natural resources, Mr. Speaker, are worthless until they are taken from the ground. The only w'ay that can be done is by the employment of capital. Capital and people are the two essential things to this country. I think even the hon. member for Last Mountain will agree to that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You mentioned capital twice. I wonder if you are forgetting labour?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I spoke of capital and people. Perhaps my hon. friend does not think that people will labour; I know many of them will not at the present time. But capital and people are what we want in this country now. Very well, you destroy the industries in the province of Quebec by lowering the tariff gradually, by not keeping those industries stable, by letting them gradually go down. If you do that how much capital do you think would come into Canada? You will not get a single dollar of the capital which is coming into this country at the present time. Place your income tax as proposed under this amendment and see how much it will help you in the way of securing capital. Why, Mr. Speaker, the income tax in this country should be reduced-there is no question about that at all. It is far too heavy a tax to put on the shoulders of the people.
If it was reduced I venture to say you would find a far greater amount of capital flowing into Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where would you get your revenue?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would get the revenue from the development tariff of which I spoke. The system of indirect taxation which is in force at the present time is the fairest way of getting a revenue. It bears equally on most people, but the direct taxation which this amendment suggests be carried out involves too heavy a load.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do you not agree that indirect taxation involves a heavy load?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Taxation of all kinds is a heavy load. Let my hon. friends opposite understand it quite clearly I am in favour of lightening taxation of every possible) form, but how can taxation be lightened at the present time with deficit after deficit in our annual budget? Indirect taxation is not pleasant, there is no question about that at all, but nevertheless there has to be taxation in order to obtain the money for running the country.
Now, I am going to depart from my Progressive friends and direct my remarks to the government itself. With a great many things my hon. friend for Brandon (Mr. Forke) has said in his speech I am in accord. I think he sized up many a situation which is well worth the most serious consideration of the government at the present time. He spoke, for example, about the question of economy. Mr. Speaker, I might be quite wrong but I think vTe are spending far too much money in this country. That, I think, is an undoubted fact. The hon. member also spoke about the cost of civil government. In my opinion he was absolutely right in his remarks in that respect. Civil government in this country is costing an outstanding, a ridiculous amount, a sum that it never should cost a little nation like ourselves. Civil government never should cost us what it costs us in Canada. Some of the figures I am about to read were taken from the speech of the hon. member for Brandon but they have been supplemented by figures of my own. In 1912 we had a population of
7.300.000,	we had 8,371 employees, and the Civil Service cost $7,805,373. In 1922, ten years later, we had a population of 8,788,000, we had 11,878 employees, and the Civil Service cost $19,271,985. So that in these ten years, although our population only increased
1.488.000,	the number of employees increased 3,507 and the cost increased $12,466,612. I sav

rites
The Budget-Mr. Marler

that expenditure for civil government in a little country like this is next to absurd, and there should be a thorough inquiry as to whether or not civil government in Canada cannot be carried on at a very much less figure. Any business would go out of existence with a lack of economy of that description.
There is another matter I intend to speak about and I apologize for keeping hon. members at this late hour. It is that we should only spend in this country what we have to spend, and cease piling up deficits year after year.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of late years we have
had a deficit each year. In 1921, $92,000,000; in 1922, $81,000,000; in 1923, $50,000,000, and possibly next year we will witness another deficit I am not criticizing the Minister of Finance; I am not even criticizing my genial friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) as regards his administration; I am criticizing every member of the House of Commons.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are wrong.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think the people
of the country will say I am wrong. They will say that this government, and any government is wrong unless we have greater economy and make our budget meet. We have got to do that. We have got to cease spending money, and the only way we shall ever be able to lighten taxation, lighten the load which is at present on the backs of the Canadian people, is to cut down our expenditure and only spend what we have got to spend.
In addition to that I have this to say: We have two classes of taxes in this country at the present time. We have our war taxes and our ordinary taxes. Our war taxes should be devoted to meeting war expenditure entirely. We have got to pay for the war and the people will cheerfully pay the taxes that are needed for that purpose. But the ordinary taxes that are levied should meet the ordinary expenditure, and the country should be rim within the limits of that taxation.
Now, Sir, I pass on to another subject and I shall not detain the House very much longer. In the budget speech there was a declaration bj' the Minister of Finance of tariff stability. That declaration has been read in a variety of ways. I, myself, thought well jf that declaration. I thought well of the intent of the minister in telling that to the manufacturers and the various other interests in the country in order that business might be stable.
.1 thought well of that declaration at the time,
^Mr. Marler.]
and I think well of it yet, because it means stability, and we do need stability without a question of doubt. But the question of tariff stability does not mean that there shall never be tariff revision in this country. We must have tariff revision in Canada. The country does not stand still. It is in the interests of the consumer and in the interests of the producer that the tariff shall be revised from time to time. Now I am going to deal once more with the word "protection" which is in this resolution which is before us. It says:
That any claim for protection should be heard publicly before a special committee of parliament.
I do not want to cast any suspicion on the committees. I do not want to deprive the members of any committee of this House of any knowledge or intelligence they should have, but I say a committee of parliament would be just about as well equipped to pass on the question of making up the tariff as it would be on the question of making up railway rates. The question of making up the tariff is one of the most complicated matters which is ever brought before parliament, and has to be dealt with by the Finance Minister. How has the tariff been made up in the past? It has been made up by a committee of ministers from the cabinet going all over the country and getting information on various questions. They no doubt did their work well. I think my hon. friend from West York headed the last commission. He no doubt did his work well. He always does his work well, the only work he does not do well is criticizing this budget, and the reason he could not criticize the budget was because he agreed almost entirely with it, and it nearly broke his heart to have to criticize it at all. That is the reason he did not do it well. I am quite certain that in the revision of the tariff he did his work very well indeed. How can even a committee of the cabinet make up a tariff?
What we need is an advisory tariff commission, which will be a permanent body, which will look into the question of the tariff, collate the necessary information and bring it forward to the Minister of Finance. I do not say that the tariff can be taken out of politics entirely. I know' that it cannot be taken out of politics altogether. I am fully aware of that fact. I know that when the tariff is made up by the advisory commission of which I speak the government of the day must have the last say as to whether or not a certain tariff shall be raised or a certain tariff shall be lowered, but I do say a body of experts can bring before the government the information which is necessary for them to make a

The Budget-Mr. Maclean (Halifax)
fair and equitable tariff and although hon. members opposite may not agree with me on the question of whether we should have what I call a development tariff or not, although they are unalterably opposed to the principle of protection, they at least would know whether the manufacturer who came forward was not getting an unreasonable protection, but that he was getting a fair protection, consistent with other interests.
Why? What has to be considered in the tariff? There is not only the question of the original cost of goods and the question of transportation, but the great question of distribution. The expense of distribution, I believe, from the manufacturer to the producer is far too much at the present time. There is a tremendous spread between what the manufacturer gets for his products and what you hon. members from the West have to pay for yours. There is no question about that. I have gone into that point time and time again with the manufacturers of Montreal. In 1912 the question of an advisory tariff commission was brought before the House of Commons; it went through the House but was defeated in the Senate. I do not think I am sufficiently narrow-minded not to accept from the Conservative party, or from the Progressive party, whatever policy is for the good of the country, because that is what we are all working for and the country is in too serious a position to put party before country. I will say on the floor of the House now that I will take advice from any party which will bring forward what is a fair and proper proposal. Therefore, recognizing the necessity of tariff revision, and speaking on the necessity of a tariff advisory commission to-night, I am glad to have the benefit of the advice which was brought before the House at the time to which I refer. The Conservatives brought this matter up in 1912, but if some hon. members on this side of the House have any objection to take advice from the Conservative party, let me say that the tariff has changed very much since 1912. In those days there was $73,000,000 collected from the tariff and now $133,000,000 is collected. Since 1912 we have had a great war and tremendous taxes have been put on our shoulders. Since 1912 we have had the pleasure of seeing that dilapidated annex of the Liberal party, namely the Progressive party, expand to the number of sixty-five. Well, sir, all these facts are true. I say the tariff should be framed with the assistance of an advisory board for the purpose of advising the Finance Minister on matters of that description, so that a fair and reasonable tariff for the development of our 194
industries and the protection of the consumer will be prepared. I regret that my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke) and the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) will not withdraw the resolution. I think they will be sorry when they get into power, which we hope will not be for a long time. When they get into power and read this resolution in Hansard I think they will have great difficulty in reconciling themselves with their action on this matter.
Let me turn to the hon. member for Brome who made a speech this evening, and stated he was absolutely against the principle and practice of protection. No doubt hon. members opposite agree with all he said. They have heard his remarks with reference to his defection. I do not intend, Mr. Speaker, to say very much about the defection of the hon. member for Brome beyond stating it was very regrettable to me that he should have adopted such an attitude towards the party he has followed for so many years. What did the hon. member say? He said he was a Liberal and he was the only man who understood the Liberal doctrine. Well, why does the hon. member for Brome pose as the arbiter of the Liberal party? Can no other hon. members in this House understand what the Liberal doctrine or the Liberal policy is? Why did he say that he, and he alone, is the only man in the House that understands the Liberal doctrine?
The hon. member for Brome is advancing his own personal ideas and views instead of sinking those personal views as many of us have to do for the general good of the country. He will not merge those views with the views of others, but he stands out for a fad and fancy and he is chasing a rainbow. That is all he is chasing when he talks about free trade. It is nothing else. It is a regrettable incident that he should take the attitude he has taken to-night. It is an impossibility to have free trade and have the country prosperous. Let me ask the hon. members opposite who applauded him so vigorously to-night, did he give you any solution of the problem as to how you were going to meet the financial obligations of the country? Did he explain to you how he was going to assist you in your policies? He did nothing at all. He did nothing at all except propound the idea that free trade was the best policy for the country, and that under the system of protection we had not been successful. I do not agree with his statement. I think we have been remarkably successful. I think our trade is certainly something to be exceedingly proud of in a country of this

The Budget-Mr. Marler

description. I think we have a splendid set of people in this country to be proud of. The effort of the West has been one of the most magnificent efforts that have ever been put forth in history. Those are all matters that we may be proud of, and they have all taken place under the system which has been in vogue for a number of years.
The hon. member for Brome went on again to speak of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He said that he knew him; that Sir Wilfrid Laurier had made him financial critic; yet he absolutely turns around on the tariff policy which Sir Wilfrid Laurier himself put into force with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), when he came into power in 1896. As a matter of fact, the Laurier-Fielding tariff is less than it was in 1896, and the hon. member for Brome says, "I revered Sir Wilfrid Laurier," yet he turns around on his follower who made the self-same tariff at that time. That is the attitude which the hon. member for Brome has taken towards the Liberal party to-night. There is no consistency in his attitude. I see the hon. member for Last Mountain shaking his head. Why does he shake his head? Will he tell me?

Some hon. gentlemen say, "hear,hear." I challenge hon. gentlemen opposite to make up any budget on the basis of free trade. I will challenge any hon. gentleman opposite, if free trade ever does come in -and it never will-to be any better off under it than under the present tariff. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould), I suppose, after voting to-morrow night, he will be sitting beside the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark). subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

We will accept the resolution on its face as being the policy of the

Progressive party. We in the East know precisely what the Progressive party in the West means, on the basis of that resolution, and that being the case, we can act accordingly.
