subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
because it is not like ordinary machinery that is kept in stock: it will have to be especially made. After that it will be necessary to instruct those who are going to use the machinery. So that I cannot see how this firm will be able to get down to business inside of three years. This is quite a large proposition, it would mean a great deal to the people of the prairies and I certainly think that the government would be fully justified in extending the period to ten years. It would mean retaining millions of dollars of Canadian money in Canada and would give work to thousands of our young people; and [DOT]what Canada wants as much as anything else is industries that will absorb our young population and give them employment. No *country can long remain in the forefront of nations whose people are not workers. I think one great necessity in Canada to-day is to provide work for the young people. Surely with a country such as we have in Canada, covering an area of 111,000 square miles, greater than the United States and Alaska combined, we should be able to find employment for Canadians. I cannot help thinking-and I am speaking in this regard from years of experience in this country- that one good Canadian bom man or woman brought up in Canada is worth two who have been brought into the country. The Canadian-born man is accustomed to Canadian ways and can help develop the country; he falls into line naturally and does his work much better than people brought from the Old Country.
There is one thing I should have liked to see in the budget and that is a little more British preference, not on goods as a whole but on clothing. When we take into consideration the amount of wheat, and cattle and other products that we sell to the Mother Country, I do think that we should give a little more preference to British-made clothing. *Canada is a cold country in the winter time, rand it is very necessary to the health of the people that they should have warm clothing; and the working people as a general rule can ill afford to pay the prices that are demanded nowadays for articles of apparel. I should have liked to see a greater reduction in that respect' than there is.
There was one question which I intended to bring up in connection with the budget, and that is the question of old age pensions. But I have been engaged to such a great extent on committees that I really have had no time to give the matter any consideration, and therefore I think I had better refrain from saying anything in reference to it. Some time ago the Minister of Labour (Mr. 
Murdock) made the statement, that he did not see that this government was under any obligation to consider any further help for the unemployed. It would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that it would be well for the hon. minister to re-consider that assertion. We in the West are in a rather peculiar position. There is generally a large floating population on the prairies that come out West in the fall of the year, and to me it hardly seems right that Vancouver-because that is the place that is most affected-should have to provide for these people in the winter time. I do not think that city should have to provide either work or food for them. Indeed, I have been always of the opinion that the Dominion government should give to the province of British Columbia special consideration in this respect. The floating population comes out West in the fall and, as I have said, as soon as the spring opens up, they drift back to the prairies and other places. We often ask ourselves this question out there, why should we provide for these people in the winter season? Yet we have got to do it. Now, I think that if the Dominion government would go ahead and construct a highway or a portion of a highway, and continue this work for a few years, as I think they would be justified in doing, it would go a long way towards relieving the situation. When British Columbia entered confederation it was agreed that the province should get a railway. Before that railway was built we had a, highway as far east as Hope; it was known as the old Cariboo road. When the railway was built it practically did away with that highway, and then the Canadian Northern was constructed and it put out of use the remainder of the highway. Generally it has been the custom when a railway is built that the railway company replaces any highways it put out of commission in the section of the country through which it passes, and I think that this government would be fully justified in replacing that portion of the highway which they were the means of destro3dng when these railways were built. If the government did this it would, as I have said, go a long way in the direction of relieving unemployment for a number of years.
Another question which I wish to touch upon briefly has reference to a statement made by Sir James Lougheed and Senator Fowler. Sir James Lougheed is reported as having said:
A change is now made, at the instance of a very small and irresponsible group in the House of Commons.

The Budget-Mr. Arthurs
I may say that he was speaking in connection with the Immigration bill.
I am satisfied that this bill does not represent the sentiments of the House, and it certainly does not represent the parliament of Canada. The small and irresponsible group in the Commons would engraft upon the statutes. . . .
He then goes on to say:
Yes, there is in the House of Commons a Labour party of one or two, I think it numbers two.
Mr. Fowler then stated:
The government showed that it had some sense in the beginning,, but then they gave way to the improper gang. We get out the worst and most dangerous agitators from the British Isles.
Sir James Lougheed interjected:
No doubt about that.
Mr. Fowler continued:
The English are a peculiar people, and if a man is attacked by the public he will be protected by the police. Then they say, "Oh, he is an Englishman," and that makes him all the more dangerous.
Now, I would like to know what right has Sir James Lougheed to make such statements about members of this House? I come from the British Isles and I have no doubt that I am one of the people referred to. If I had not at least as good a record as Sir James Lougheed or Mr. Fowler I do not think I would want to sit in the House of Commons. It seems to me that no man is a true Canadian who does not want to build up in Canada a great white civilization with brotherly friendship as its guiding star. I go further and say that I think such statements' as those which I have quoted show a lack of principle that one might not expect to find in a gentleman; nor do I think a gentleman would make such statements about any member of this House, and I for one resent it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Before discussing the budget, Mr. Speaker, I desire to add my congratulations to those already tendered the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) upon the introduction of his eighteenth budget. I think other members have referred to it as the seventeenth, but if my memory serves me last session the hon. gentleman introduced practically two budgets, so one may say that this is his eighteenth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The seventeenth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The eighteenth I think.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to five or six, as the case may be, of those budgets. I have also listened to the hon. gentleman in opposition when he was the chief financial critic for his party, and I can assure him that he makes a better critic than he does a minister of finance so far as his budgets are concerned. I only hope he may long continue to be active in one of those two capacities,-preferably as financial critic of the opposition.
When the budget of 1922 was brought down the country awaited it with great interest. Almost everybody in Canada was anxious to hear the budget debate of that year, for they were eager to know whether the government would fulfil the promises contained in their 1919 platform and supplemented by various speeches from members of the government. But the friends of the government were disappointed. They found that this "immediate and general reduction of duties" as promised in the platform of 1919 did not materialize. They found that farm implements were not placed upon the free list, and that mill machinery and other implements of production were still on the old tariff basis. In a word, they found that none of the articles specifically mentioned in the platform of 1919 were put on the free list-not even cement. My right hon. friend, the Prime Minister, did me the honour to invade my constituency, and while the Minister of Finance says he did not subscribe to the platform of 1919, I can assure him quite confidently that his leader while in my county did subscribe to every plank of that platform in so many words.
It is quite true that in order to please our friends from the West there was a reduction made of 2i per cent in the duty on certain farm implements, but every cent of this was accounted for by an increase in the sales tax, so that to-day the farmer of the West has not benefited one cent by the reduction in duty. During the election of 1921 in my county, and I think in every other county in Ontario, our friends opposite held up the duty on boots and shoes as a horrible example of what a tariff might amount to. They took the duty of 30 per cent and pyramided it in various ways until they had it over 100 per cent; but we do not find that since our friends succeeded to office they have made any attempt to reduce this duty.
They also took various other ways of implementing their promises. For instance, they made a reduction of 5 per cent on milk bottles and also upon their paper covers, and they made porcelains for pumps absolutely free. That was the total extent of tariff reductions during 1922. But to offset this they increased our taxation in various; ways. As I have already intimated they increased the sales tax of 50 per cent and allowed it to pyramid in exactly the same way as before, with the result that for the last fiscal year they have collected approximately
The Budget-Mr. Arthurs

$31,000,000 more than they would have under the old rate. They also placed an additional tax upon cheques and upon receipts. The latter, Mr Speaker, is a very grievous and annoying burden upon the people of this country. If a drover comes along to a fanner and makes him a payment of $10 or $15 upon a purchase of cattle, the farmer is supposed to be able to immediately produce a two-cent stamp and place it upon his receipt.
I notice that the minister has seen fit to reduce the tax upon cheques. Last* session after considerable discussion he agreed that the tax should not be greater than two dollars; in other words, that cheques for $5,000 should go through for two dollars apiece. This year he has reduced that to $1 maximum. But the poor man who issues small cheques is still taxed in exactly the same way.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I suppose the rich man .gives many a small cheque?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And he pays the tax; but if he gives a big cheque he gets off at half price.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If he gives a small cheque he helps the poor man to pay the tax.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why not let him pay the whole tax? It is just as reasonable that he should pay the same proportion of tax on cheques that he does on his income.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is quite another matter. My hon. friend wanted to make the poor man out as being the only issuer of small cheques, which is absurd.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What I say is that the tax is infinitely more on the poor man who issues small cheques than on the rich man who issues big cheques. The net result of the tariff of 1922 was to increase duties by three-quarters of one per cent on dutiable goods in another way, the net result was to increase the duty on all goods entering Canada, whether free or dutiable, by one-third of one per cent. But the friends of our friends opposite said, "This government has only been in power a few months.' They cannot do everything in a day; the best solution is to leave them alone for a year and wait until they bring down the budget of 1923." Well, we are here to-day to discuss the tariff of 1923. I am quite satisfied that our free trade friends, if we have any, outside of one hon. member who spoke this evening-I am quite satisfied that our Progressive friends, too, are disappointed, and that they find very little comfort in this budget of 1923. It is quite true there are certain small reductions. The minister has 
reduced the duty upon goods entering Canada from Great Britain by an average of 1-^ to 2J per cent, and outside of certain specific articles, I do not know that I quarrel with him in that respect; I think his intention was a good one. His idea seems to be to promote trade through Canadian ports, and so far as that is concerned I hold up both hands in favour of the minister's position. However,. there are certain articles-the woollen trade has already been brought to the attention of the minister-in connection with which the proposed change will entail great hardship. I am not going to take up the time of the House on that point; the minister knows the situation just as well as I do; he knows the difficulty that may ensue in that connection.
The minister has also reduced the duty on sugar by 50 cents a hundred. The average householder purchases in a year less than 200 pounds of sugar. The minister stated that the reduction in duty would amount to $1,250,000. I think I am correct in that figure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Two and a half millions.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, any figure you like. This reduction is principally to manufacturers of candies and various lines of that kind. I have said that the average householder consumes less than 200 pounds of sugar annually; that would mean a reduction to him of one dollar per year. The minister in the next line of his tariff is adding to the duty on currants and raisins-multiplying it, in fact, by 41. He has increased it by 450 per cent- from two-thirds of a cent to 3 cents a pound. The housewife, therefore, will pay in the increased duty on currants and raisins every cent of the reduction on sugar.
The minister has also made a small reduction on scrap iron. I do not know whether or not that affects our friends from the West, but these are the only reductions of any moment in the tariff proposals of the minister. He is very careful to see that nothing but what is really scrap comes into the country, under the conditions of the amended tariff.
But the minister has also increased the duty in many ways, particularly on the ingredients that go into the manufacture of paint. In spite of the hon. minister's declaration of some years ago that he was not in favour of establishing any new industries in Canada at the expense of the taxpayer; that if a man undertook to establish a new industry and expected to have protection for it, his advice to him was, "Don't,"-I am not

The Budget-Mr. Arthurs
quoting his exact words, but I am giving the tenor of his remarks-in spite of that he has introduced duties which have been so far unheard of in Canada, though I am not saying that they are wrong. The first on the list is a duty of 35 cents per hundred pounds on potatoes. I think the hon. minister is right in doing that; he would be right if he followed the whole line of the Fordney tariff and gave our American friends some of the medicine they are trying to give us. But the minister did not enunciate that principle in years gone by; this procedure is contrary to his former declarations in this House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He has enunciated it now.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He has had a change of heart. If he really feels that change of heart he should be on the other side of the House.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How would you like him over there?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What pledges?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tariff pledges. Perhaps there was an exception in the case of the province of Quebec, but hon. gentlemen went all over the country from the boundaries of the province of Quebec to Vancouver preaching lower duties, proclaiming that their tariff was exactly the same as that of our Progressive friends, and they were elected on that stand. They have repudiated that; to-day, as I have said, they have a tariff which is higher than the tariff they found in effect when they came into power.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman name one authoritative Liberal who preached that during the campaign?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister
preached it in my riding.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As I heard it from all the leaders-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am making this speech. The hon. gentleman has got my answer. There is one thing I overlooked to mention. The government did make an attempt to lower the cost of living, and they did it in this way: They arranged and presented to this House a treaty with France, whereby they give important concessions to that country-especially low duties on wines, silks, laces, handkerchiefs, ribbons, millinery, etc. The farmer and the workingman will be pleased to know that the duty on silk has been reduced to 20 per cent, while the duty on printed and dyed cotton fabrics remains at 25, 30 and 324 per cent in respect to all other countries. They have reduced the duty on velvets from 324 to 20 per cent; on French laces from 274 per cent to 15 per cent; on perfumery from 32 per cent to 25 per cent; on feathers and ornaments for hats, from 274 to 224 per cent. And in respect to all these items the reductions apply not only to France but to Switzerland, Japan and various other countries under the favoured nation clause. I may point out that it is a good way to lose revenue but a very poor way to reduce the cost of living. Every dollar of revenue that is lost owing to the negotiation of this treaty 

and it will amount to upwards of a million dollars-must be paid in some way, and it will be made up by the man who is subject to direct taxation; there is no question about that. I am sure that our prohibition friends -they have not any in Quebec, I presume,
The Budget-Mr. Arthurs

but elsewhere there are some-will be pleased to know that the minister has reduced the excise duty on native wines from 30 cents to 7i cents per gallon, or from 6 cents to li cents a bottle. I am quite sure that Mr. Raney will agree with the minister in that particular.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Raney approves of it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you sure of that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Native wine is provided for in his act.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I want to say a word in regard to the 6 per cent sales tax. The minister has claimed that the new tax will not be pyramided. Well, as a matter of straight business, the tax of 6 per cent upon the manufacturer will, before it reaches the retailer, be upwards of 10 per cent. We will take it that the average rate of profit from the manufacturer to the jobber or wholesaler is 20 per cent upon the original cost of the goods. That will increase this sales tax from $6 to $7.20. The usual profit to the retailer is 33 1/3 per cent or upwards. If we take it at an average of 33 1/3 per cent we find that the tax when it reaches the consumer amounts to $9.60 instead of $6. Or in other words for every $6 of money that the government receives the consumer pays $9.60.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words upon an entirely different matter. The government have not stated to parliament what their attitude will be regarding the Crowsnest pass agreement in the future. We have a provisional arrangement putting the Crowsnest pass agreement into operation. It has been in effect for one year during which time the railway companies claim they have suffered a loss in receipts of $20,000,000. Now I contend that every dollar of that is at the expense of the eastern shipper. Before the Crowsnest pass agreement was put into force last year the railway companies approached parliament, and the country, and offered a reduction of approximately 7i per cent on all basic articles. This would give a fairer rate upon lumber, brick, cement, and all kinds of farm products both in the'East and in the; West. Northern Ontario, from which I come depends largely upon the production of lumber, pulp-wood, ties, etc., the production of which furnishes employment for thousands of men. The hon. member who spoke immediately before me commended the minister for placing a bounty upon copper, on the ground that it would employ from 500 to 1,000 men. I can safely say that the tie and pulp industries in northern Ontario employ ten times that
TMr. Arthurs.]
number of men every year, and in many years twice that number. During the war, and since, the rates upon these various articles have been increased by 100 per cent. To-day we find in northern Ontario that where the men previously received $80 to $90 a month with board-and I am speaking of northern Quebec just as much as northern Ontario- they now receive from $26 to $35 per month and board. We find that the farmer up there, who is *he principal producer of pulpwood, is faced with a condition that leaves him in very poor shape financially. We all know that the price of lumber, ties, pulpwood, and other materials of this nature is fixed at the point of delivery. Well, the farmer receives that price but it is a fact that in many cases in northern Ontario he pays more for freight rates upon this lumber than he receives for the timber, for his work upon that timber upon his piling, loading and everything else included. These are absolute facts, and I believe that in the interest of this country, something should be done to relieve these men from the present condition which is almost intolerable.
Now I want to say a few words upon the immigration question.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am away from the tariff question now. I want to point out that in 1914, before the war, our immigration amounted to 403,000. In 1920, soon after the war finished, it amounted to 117,000, in 1921 it was 148,000, and last year, 89,000, steadily dropping as hon. members will notice
The Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Stewart), when he explained his policy the other day, brought forward no solution of the immigration question. His main effort, apparently, was to hand over -I was going to say to some private individuals but it is not necessarily so-to some company $100,000 provided they induced 200 families to settle upon land in western Canada ; or in other words to give them a bonus of $500 per family. I can assure him that if he hands that money over to even the Drury government we will get better results than that in Ontario alone. I listened with a great deal of interest to the debate on* immigration. I did not speak, but I found there were as many opinions expressed as there were members speaking, and they were not all confined to one side of the House. On the government side there were-I will not say renegades-but some men who at least were not in favour of the policy as announced by the government.

Tht Budget-Mr. Arthurs

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who were they?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler), the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). These were the notable and upstanding figures on the government side.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who said that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. members referred to said it themselves. They said they were opposed to the policy of the government. The difference of opinion among the members of the Progressive party was even worse than among the members on the government side. We found the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) saying that we should have all the immigrants we could and he would not confine them to agriculturists, he wanted mechanics and artisans. The hon. members behind him entered into what I might almost call a Marathon to see who could make the darkest and worst picture of the conditions in their own particular county. I am quite certain that I never heard before in this House-even in the old days when the Liberals were in opposition and used to use some strong expressions about the conditions of the country-I never heard a more depressing speech, or one of such a blue ruin character, than that made by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) wherein he said that there were already in his province 20,000 bankrupt and the rest were going through as fast as they could. The only bon. member, in my opinion, who beat him as a blue ruin artist was the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good). He said that if we wanted men to go on the farm we ought to import Asiatics, that they were the only men who would stay there at the present time, and he commended that policy to the government apparently in all earnestness. Our friends in Toronto have a different policy. They are going through the country to-day claiming that they have a policy which will put men on the farm only. As a matter of fact I read in a newspaper, either to-day or yesterday, that some men imported from Stornoway under this policy had gone into some other employment-I will not say what it was-and the provincial government were going to deport them because they did not stay on the farm. It was a brewery.
I was glad to hear the statement of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr- Motherwell) that he was at the present time paying attention to the northern parts of Ontario and Quebec. I come from northern Ontario, and I may tell hon. members of this House that
there are millions of acres of land there available at the present time, which will make the finest homesteads in Canada. Some of this land is timbered and some is burnt over. Preferably the best land is the timbered land. That will probably seem strange to our western friends, but the timber on the land provides work for the men during the winter and gives them an income, so they can go ahead and clean up the soil. The best residents of Canada are the men in these northern districts. While the agricultural population of Ontario has been decreasing in most parts, the agricultural population of northern Ontario has been increasing each and every census, and will continue to increase, and I think it would be wise if the minister would make an effort to populate that part of the country. I commend the minister for his consideration in the matter. We do not grow wheat up there, but the man who grows the most wheat is the poorest man, according to the theories of my hon. friends to the left of me. No part of Ontario is better adapted for cattle raising or ordinary mixed farming than this district. It is quite true that some of these men have suffered misfortunes on account of fires, but we find them going ahead and rebuilding their homes, and a year from now they will be in better position than before the fire, because the land will have been burnt over and cleaned.
I remember thirty years ago we had a slump in ^he lumber market in northern Ontario, and many of the men from my county left their farms in the Parry Sound district and went west, most of them going to Alberta. To-day there is not one of those farms that is not in better condition than when these men left it. Our farmers are succeeding. Many men have come in, have occupied the farms for a while, have turned the farms over to their sons and have retired to small villages having made enough to keep them according to their ideas. I think this matter should be brought more prominently to the attention of those incoming settlers whom we hope to receive in Canada. The hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) said that he quite agreed with the minister in certain particulars, but he thought they required a different class of settlers. He said if we had to populate northern Ontario or northern Quebec wTe should have the men who would lead the simple life. I do not know whether in the West they lead a double life or not; if they do, perhaps that will account for some of their troubles. But I can assure him that conditions in northern Ontario are just as good in every way as in other parts of the
3038	, COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Denis (St. Denis)
country. We have roads, schools and everything that the West can offer the settler- even Ford cars.
As I said before, I am in favour of an immigration policy of this kind.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this debate has
begun, many speeches have been made, many views have been expressed, but I think this discussion, which is not lacking in importance, would have been better appreciated by the country, if the speakers had restricted themselves to the subject matter of the budget. Unfortunately, such was not the case. The interests at large were sacrificed, or rather relegated to the back ground, for the benefit of a certain group, a certain class, or a portion of the country to the detriment of the public's interests. Are these, Sir, the duties incumbent on a loyal representative of the people? I do not think so, and if a number of members are guided by such ideas they have a wrong conception of their responsibilities. I was much impressed by the eloquent speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Finance. His excellent work calls for my most sincere congratulations. He is truly the man of the hour-the best man in the right place. If the country enjoyed an era of prosperity under the regime of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, between 1896 and 1911, it is due to the hon. Minister of Finance, the same person who, at present, is in our midst. From 1911 to 1921, the Conservative party was at the helm of the affairs of the country, with the result you all know. The country was beset by many evils. Not satisfied with having increased our national debt by hundreds of millions or having burdened the people with heavy taxes, they forced, through an infamous and anti-Canadian Act, our sons to cross the seas to shed their blood on the plains of Europe. While this was going on our Ministers-a few of their silhouettes I notice on the cold benches of the opposition-were scattering the public moneys in the name of freedom and civilization under the double cloak of war and the British flag.
On December 6, 1921, the day of relief came, forever honoured in the history of our beautiful country. The people, aroused and disgusted, drove from power these ravenous wolves so as to bring back to power the country's former benefactors.
Barely a few months have elapsed since the Liberal party, under the wise and progressive-not progressist-direction of its leader, the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, took hold of the administration of the country, that the clouds which darkened the horizon are scattering, unveiling a ray of hope, 
to the great satisfaction of the people of this country. There is considerable improvement in the financial situation, thanks to the wisdom, experience and ability of the hon. Minister of Finance. The period of deficits is coming to an end and would already be a thing of the past had we not inherited from the late regime the National Railways and Merchant Marine which alone absorb 1100,000,000 of our revenues per year.
Thanks to the economy being now practised, before long the budget will balance itself and the taxes imposed through the necessity of the moment will, to the satisfaction of all, disappear. I deem it my duty to congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance for having made progress in that direction, in relieving us of certain taxes on the necessities of life, thus lightening the burden of the consumer, and allowing industries which employ a great number of hands, to better remunerate them. I wish further to extend to him our thanks for having suppressed the retail sales tax so as to collect it at the source of production and on imports.
Before resuming my seat, Mr. Speaker, there is one subject to which I want to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Finance: it is the income tax.
To be brief and so as not to take up the time of the House with useless repetitions, I shall simply state that I entirely approve the few suggestions which were put forth by the hon. member for Chambly-Vercheres (Mr. Archambault). I favour giving an exemption of $500 instead of $300 for each child. I am in favour of exempting the head of a family of all taxes on a revenue of less than $5,000.
I support the suggestion of allowing an exemption for all children who are going through a course of study. I would also like to see a tax on dividends drawn from all investments in companies, wholly apart from the tax already imposed on the general business of these companies. The husband and wife having property in common should each benefit of an exemption of $2,000; in a word, they should be looked upon as if they were separated as to property, according to the spirit of the Income Tax Act.
I feel confident that the hon. minister will give to these few suggestions his serious consideration and that a bill purporting to such an arrangement will meet with the general assent of this House.
One last word, Mr. Speaker, I have full confidence that the present government will know how to carry on efficiently the country's affairs. I confide in their sense of justice and patriotism and for those reasons, I shall vote

The Budget-Mr. Leader
against the amendment and in favour of the main motion.
In giving such a vote, I am absolutely satisfied that I will have done my duty towards my country and the electors that I have the honour of representing.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am certainly not desirous of rising to make a speech at this late hour, but I have a duty to perform. I have the advantage of hon. members who have been in constant attendance in this House, in the fact that I have been able to go home and have a week's vacation on the farm. While that is an advantage, in that I feel fresh in comparison with some hon. members present, it is a disadvantage as well because what I have to say may be a repetition, as I was not in this House to listen to the speeches and I have not had time to read them. If, however, I wander far afield, I know Mr. Speaker will call me to order.
While I was in the West, news of the budget that had'been delivered here had travelled that far, and the man or the woman is a rare bird, indeed, who is in favour of the budget as it was brought down this year. The western people are almost a unit, so far as I can see or hear, in condemning this budget that was delivered in 1923. This morning I received a resolution passed by the District Board of the constituency of Portage la Prairie, and I should like to read it to the House, if hon. members will bear with me. It reads:
Portage la Prairie, May 19, 1923. Mr. H. Leader, M.P.,
Parliament Bldgs.,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Sir:
I am instructed by the district Board of the Constituency of Portage la Prairie to forward to you the following.
Whereas the national prosperity is mainly dependent on the development of those interests native to the country, and whereas a tariff based on the principles of protection bears unduly on those natural industries thus retarding production and the development of our natural resources, to the point that agriculture can scarcely maintain itself and is becoming completely demoralized, and whereas the present government gave definite promise in its platform of 1919 to remove the duty on at least the necessities of life and the implements of production. Therefore be it resolved that we recognize the tariff proposals of the Hon. Mr. Fielding as breaking faith with the people of Canada, and further we stand unalterably opposed to the principle of protection being recognized in formulating tariff proposals. And we further express our wholehearted approval of the amendment proposed by Mr. Forke, leader of the Progressives.
James McKenzie.
Mr. James McKenzie is one of the old-time Liberals of Portage plains. I think I am safe
in saying that on this committee of seventeen or twenty-one, I do not know which, not more than two members are not former Liberals; they all condemn the budget that has been brought down, and they are firmly of opinion that the Liberal party has betrayed the people of this country.
There are in the budget things that we could, perhaps, say a good word for. I should like to say-and when I say this, I know it will not meet with the approval of many of my Progressive colleagues-that as a good Canadian I approve the preference for British goods entering Canada via Canadian ports. The government might have carried out that part of their platform very easily at this time. I think they should increase the British preference to at least 50 per cent. They have a great opportunity in view of the fact that Britain has come to our aid and lifted the embargo in order to allow our cattle to enter the Old Country. The government might have reciprocated and increased the British preference to 50 per cent in accordance with their platform. My idea would be to work the duty off altogether and to admit British goods into Canada via Canadian ports duty free.
There is one phase in connection with this budget that I should like to see rectified, and that is as regards the stamp tax. Last year when the grain dealers were buying wheat from the 'Canadian farmers, in the settlement for grain they issued their cheques; they put stamps on them, and they charged the stamps back to the farmers. This was the cause of considerable annoyance and there was a great deal of opposition to it. In my own case I did not like it. It was not universal; they could not say that it was a rule of the Grain Exchange, because they violated that rule many times. The first car I sold to Smith-Murphy, they either forgot to charge the stamp tax back, or they did not think it worth while to do so. As regards the second car, in sending me back settlement, they charged me up with the stamps. I wrote them saying that I felt inclined to contest this right, and they wrote back claiming that they had every right in the world to do so. I went to a lawyer thinking that we would make a test case, and I was advised by the lawyer that unless I had plenty of money to spend, it would, perhaps, be better to drop the matter. That is rather unusual advice from a lawyer. I was advised to write to the law officers of the Crown in Ottawa. I did so, and after consideration on their part, I received a letter in reply stating that there was no doubt that the law called for stamps to be placed on every cheque, but that the question
The Budget-Mr. Leader

as to who should pay for the stamps was a matter of settlement between the parties interested. This simply meant that I had no redress in that direction unless I went into a lawsuit. I then took the matter up with the Board of Grain Commissioners at Fort William, and while I will not read all of the letter I received in reply, it says in part:
In reply to your inquiry of November 1st, I have to advise that the matter referred to therein does not come within the jurisdiction of this board.
What I should like to know is who has jurisdiction over this matter. If any organization or body in this country can issue a cheque, put stamps on it and compel the other fellow to pay for the stamps, that looks to me like special privilege. I should like to know if the Grain Exchange has this special privilege. If it has, we want to know that fact, and I do not think it should enjoy that privilege.
I should like for a few moments to speak about the cattle trade. I might say that I am a practical cattle raiser; I have put a good deal of money into the business, and I am desirous of raising for export the very best class of steers that I possibly can. We have hopes of increasing the revenues from our farm by going into the live stock business. It, however, rather takes the heart out of a man when he has reached that stage of investing his hard-earned capital in an industry and when he is producing what the market demands, to find some big interest step in and take the cream off. That has happened as regards our freight rates. The lifting of the embargo should mean a great stimulus to stock breeding but ocean rates are too high, and they are robbing the farmers of their legitimate profits. A lower tariff should be established and maintained by the action of the government. I see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is in his seat. I notice on reading Hansard that he says:
The reason I take this matter up now is because on several occasions there have been intimations of a more or less insinuating character made with respect to this matter. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) came out frankly and intimated gross negligence on the part of the Department of Agriculture with respect to this matter.
I did say that, and I think I could prove the charge. The Minister of Agriculture made the statement that he had inquired of Sir Henry Thornton and had been told that it would take at least $32,000 to fit up each ship to take our cattle overseas. Let me quote from the Winnipeg Free Press of May 17:
But if Mr. Motherwell had this information, why did his deputy as late as December 13, 1922, make I Mr. Leader.]
this statement to the members of the Western Canada Live-Stock Union-
Who met in Brandon last winter.
-"Canada owns a number of vessels and I have been trying to influence the department to put some of these vessels at the disposal of the cattle interests. I hope the government will make a move in the matter. These vessels are not very large, nor are they as seaworthy as they might be, but they could be utilized in the spring and fall trade."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Dr. Grisdale, my deputy, made the statement, which he is reported to have made, in December, before Sir Henry Thornton was in charge, while Sir Henry Thornton's statement was made in March. That is the difference.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Evidently the department had under consideration the question of fixing up the vessels to take care of the trade. As I said before, I think I could substantiate ' the charge I made in this matter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member meant it very seriously. It was just a little play in the game.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I might point out that in a newspaper report it was stated that even the dumb beasts themselves objected to the attitude of the government, for the very first steer that landed on the other side upset the representative of the government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps they had been celebrating.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I happened to see a letter written by the president of the Scottish Farmers' Union-Mr. Elliott, I believe the gentleman's name is-in which he stated that $160,000,000 was paid for Irish cattle last year.
I think that Canada might very well get a share of this trade.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not think that there is necessarily a difference between the statement of Dr. Grisdale and that of the Minister of Agriculture.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If there is a difference, it is this, that the deputy did try to persuade the government as late as last December, and the government had cognizance of the fact, that we needed vessels. The Deputy Minister of Agriculture was trying to induce them to get those vessels ready to take care of the trade that would open up this spring.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister said that they could be utilized. The Minister of Agriculture found out that they could be utilized but at great cost.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend (Mr. Leader) be good enough to tell us

The Budget-Mr. Leader
wherein I was remiss in my duty in this matter? I know he does not want to be unfair.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have no desire whatever to be disrespectful, for I have every admiration for the Minister of Agriculture; but I rather think that he himself has been playing politics so far as this question is concerned. I see by Hansard that he made the statement that it was owing to the advertising of the number of cattle that we were going to ship overseas that the shipowners put up their rates. Well, if anyone did any boosting it was Mr. Duncan Marshall, the representative of the government, who went over to England and made the statement that at least

speechtext:
I thunk the Minister of Agriculture should quit playing politics in this matter, should put away all camouflage, and make an honest-to-goodness attempt to foster this great branch of the live stock industry.
I would bring to the attention of the House the question of the recent floods in Manitoba. This is almost an annual occurrence in my constituency, where the Assiniboine river overflows its banks. There have been some delegations here to interview the government and I have been in touch with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King, Kootenay) myself. A telegram was sent to me the other day concerning this matter, which I shall read to the House. It is from the secretary of the Elie branch of the United Farmers:
A meeting was held to discuss flood conditions on May 12th 1923 at Dacotah Man. of farmers and even in spite of conditions of roads caused by flood the farmers of the district were well represented. After a general discussion of seriousness of flood conditions caused by over-flow of Assiniboine river the following resolution was passed:
"Be it resolved that in view of the immense damage caused on the south side of the Assiniboine river, and this being the second flood in two weeks flooding thousand of acres each time the area covered being at least fifteen miles long and several miles wide, and this being a repetition of last year when land was covered with water after crop was in causing suffering and ruin to farmers, most farmers having to move out for first flood, having feed and seed ruined, then moving back and seeding, and then having the second flood, thousand of acres will not be reseeded this year, and in this instance the flooded condition being over seven miles from the river and this being only fractional part of damages, this meeting urges that the government do something to remedy the situation."
In regard to the condition of affairs out there, I am of the opinion, as I stated last year to the Minister of Public Works of the province of Manitoba as well as to the federal minister, that concerted action should be taken to meet the situation. This is a matter that calls for the consideration of the municipalities, which I think should work in conjunction with the provincial and the federal governments. I believe that they could arrive at some plan of concerted action that would provide adequate measures to cope with this annual difficulty.
I want to say a word in regard to the' National Railways, which constitute one of the biggest items of our expenditure. The only solution for our railway problem is more traffic and efficient management. The people are realizing this and are giving the National Railways more and more patronage, while the employees are anxious to give good service so that the railways may pay. Going home a short time ago I fell in with a gentleman who was just coming back from England. I might observe, by the way, that I never miss an opportunity of seeking information in regard to our National Railways, and I got into conversation with this gentleman. He had been in this country for thirteen years and he told me that he was a booster for the Canadian National Railway system. He said that in Great Britain this government, as previous governments had done, was maintaining an immigration office to secure immigrants to Canada. When any immigrant went to the office he inquired how he would travel if he wanted to get to Battleford, Winnipeg, Calgary, Edmonton or any other centre in Canada. The immigration agent would inform him that there were two railway systems in this country, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railway, both first-class. The emigrant goes home and the next day gets a stack of circulars from the Canadian Pacific Railway glorifying that system. Of course, we admire them for this, because they are after the business; but the fact is that the emigrant gets not one word with regard to the Canadian National Railways. I am not criticizing our railways, but I hope that whatever I say in this respect, which is intended for the benefit of the system, will be taken into consideration and be accepted in the proper spirit, and that if there are any irregularities they will be rectified at once. Owing to a slight accident on the road we were three hours late getting into Winnipeg. This man had his wife and two daughters and an aged mother, eighty years old, whom he went to England to bring out to this coun-
The Budget-Mr. Leader

try. We had to be transferred from the train we were on to another train over about a quarter of a mile of rooky country, and it will be readily understood what a trial this was for the aged lady. We were three hours late arriving at Winnipeg. The conductor of the train told these good people that as they were billed right through to Vancouver they would not have to be transferred to another car in Winnipeg and could go to bed. Arriving in Winnipeg orders were given to transfer them to another car, and this old lady, who had been in bed about two and a half hours, had again to be disturbed. There was another woman with three small children of four years, two years and three months respectively, and these, too, had to be transferred to another car. The confusion may be imagined.

speechtext: Will my hon. friend give me the date?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It would be a week ago Sunday night. What I am trying to get at is that people will patronize the road that gives them service. When this man arrived in Winnipeg, he said, "I have been a booster for the Canadian National System, but I have been sold." He did not go so far as to say he was through with the system, but he was evidently very much disgusted. The conductors were not to blame, it was some one higher up. I do not want to get anyone into trouble, but I am anxious to see our railways given a fair chance. Some of the passengers on that train inquired if they had time to go down to a restaurant to get something to eat, and they were advised by some of the officials that the train would be despatched as soon as possible. They waited for a time, and then they were informed that it would not go out until twelve o'clock. When they got down to the restaurant they found it closed.

speechtext:
Perhaps that is customary; anyway it was not conducive to a good frame of mind among these people. I find the equipment of the Canadian National Railway is just as good as that of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the employees are just as anxious as their rivals to make everyone comfortable. In a word they are trying to get business for the people's system. And I believe that the people in general are beginning to realize that they must patronize their own road if they ever expect to have it on a paying basis. We admire the Canadian Pacific Railway, but we have got to give the public just as good service on our national system if we are going

to get their patronage. I went to the trouble of finding out how many cattle have been shipped from Winnipeg since the British embargo was lifted, and how they were routed. I found that over twelve hundred were transported by the Canadian Pacific Railway and around nine hundred by the Canadian National. The Canadian Pacific are getting the business. I was told by a man who claimed he knew the facts that twenty-five carloads of Canadian cattle that should have been shipped over the Canadian National Railway were switched at the last moment to the Canadian Pacific Railway at Winnipeg. I am offering these criticisms not to knock our national railway, but to build up the system and see if we cannot convert these deficits into surpluses.
What I have now to say will interest the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock). Does he remember Riley's army? This has a vital connection with the revenue of our railways. Some members of the government have stated they are not in favour of public ownership, while other ministers have said, "We are willing to give public ownership of our railways a trial. It is a legacy bequeathed to us by the previous government* and we will do our best with it." Well, last year Riley's army marched down to Ottawa. They were transported back to Toronto not over the Canadian National Railway but over the Canadian Pacific. The Minister of Labour will correct me if I am wrong, but I understand a special train from Ottawa to Toronto costs $800.

There was a very substantial reason for sending Riley's army back to Toronto by the Canadian Pacific Railway-a reason which I am sure the hon. member would admit to be am pi j if he knew the facts.

speechtext:
The point I want to make is that this money was paid to the Canadian Pacific Railway when it might have gone into the revenues of the people's railway. This system should pay very shortly if we all

The Budget-Mr. Leader
do our duty by it. We hear quite a lot about government interference with the management of the Canadian National Railways, but I do not see how we can give Sir Henry Thornton a free hand so long as we are footing the bill. That is why I am addressing these remarks to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), who I hope will take them into consideration and see if he cannot prevent the repetition of such mistakes. Other matters have come under my personal observation, but I do noc deem it wise to make them public here tonight. However, I shall be very pleased to have an interview with the minister and convey this further information to him with a view to getting things fixed up.
What I am about to say now will not be very popular. In view of the fact that our public debt was increased nearly fifty million dollars this year, and is very likely to be increased to about the same extent next year, I want to declare that the government plea for economy is not sincere. I will tell you why. I introduced a resolution some time ago, and hon. members know with what favour it was met. I do not say that opposition came all from the other side of the House. But I do know that the government are creating new offices and paying out high salaries, and if they were honestly anxious 1o economize they would not do this. I need mention only two specific cases-Mr. Duncan Marshall's appointment at a salary of $6,000 a year and expenses of $15 a day; and Dr. Pugsley's at a salary of $9,000 a year.

I had quite an experience
when I introduced my resolution for the reduction of indemnities and I am convinced that it is no use for a private member to introduce such a resolution. Economies along these lines must come from the government; they must have the endorsation of the government. Yesterday a Conservative member-I forget his name-and to-night the hon. member for St. Lawrence division (Mr. Marler), suggested that there was too much extravagance in the administration of the affairs of the country. The hon. member to my right declared that there were three or four cabinet ministers absent during the session at the very
time their presence was needed in Ottawa, if it was ever needed here. But you are getting along quite well, and I think you can do it always. The United States only has ten cabinet ministers, and I do not believe they are a bit better than you people are. I think we could get along here with ten, too.

I would like to congratu- " late the Manitoba Free Press, that journal that the Minister of Agriculture seems to take exception to. I want to congratulate the manager, whoever is in charge-I do not know who is. There was_ a time when I was not in sympathy with the doctrines taught by the Free Press or with the men who guided its policy. I understand that Sir Clifford Sifton is still guiding the destinies of the Free Press, and I want to take this opportunity of congratulating him for the stand he is taking for the common people of this country.
Canada, in common with other countries, is crying out for honest men to guide and guard her destiny, and that destiny is what God meant it to be-a great free British commonwealth, inhabited by a prosperous and contented people.
